speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister).
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DEATH OF MR. JOHN McINTOSH, M.P.
speechtext:
The press has already informed the members of this House that it has been our misfortune to lose one of our colleagues, in the person of Mr. John McIntosh, member for the city of Sherbrooke. Mr. McIntosh has been carried away after a severe illness which had lasted for many years ; in fact, when Mr. McIntosh entered this House, some four years ago, he was already suffering from the illness which finally caused

his death, and at that time, as I am personally aware, it was only his strong attachment to his party and his long and well-deserved popularity in the city of Sherbrooke, which induced him-nay, rather compelled him-to accept the candidature and become a member of this House. Under such circumstances, it was not possible for Mr. McIntosh, as a member of this House, to give us the full measure of his abilities or to enable us to judge what sort of man he was. I do not believe that even to his friends on the other side of the House the real man was fully known. Perhaps in this sense I was more privileged than many of his political friends, because for a great many years it was my personal privilege to know him-I will not say intimately-but, at all events, sufficiently, I think, to he counted as among Mr. McIntosh's friends. It will be eighteen years next fall since I first met Mr McIntosh. I then met him during a contest in the eastern townships, which was bitterly fought-if that expression is not too strong-between the two parties in the province of Quebec. I had then the privilege of meeting Mr. McIntosh many and many a time, and then and there I formed the highest possible estimate of his character. At that time, I may say without exaggeration, he was a perfect type of manhood, physical manhood, and manhood in every sense of the word. Nor am I at all exaggerating when I say that I do not think I ever met a more honourable man. It is with all my heart that I associate myself with the mourning of his friends and of his family.

maintopic: DEATH OF MR. JOHN McINTOSH, M.P.
speechtext:
I thank the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Uaurier) very much for the very appropriate and kindly words which he has uttered in regard to Mr. McIntosh. The lamented death of that gentleman has caused many regrets, not only on this side of the House, but, I am sure, on the other side as well. Mr. McIntosh had filled many important public positions in this country, and it is true, as -the Prime Minister has said, that we have not seen him at his best in parliament, owing to the suffering which he continually endured from the fatal disease which eventually carried him off in the prime of life. His entry into this parliament was, I believe, induced by the most absolutely unselfish and patriotic motives. He came here against his will at a time when he felt that the interests of his country and of his party demanded that he should do so. Since his entry into parliament I have always found him a faithful colleague and a true and unselfish friend. I believe that the public life of Canada has not produced any better or higher type of public man than that which John McIntosh exemplified. He endured his illness with characteristic fortitude and with true Christian resignation. It is only a day or two since I received a letter from him, in which he spoke in the most calm and philosophical manner of the sufferings he Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
was enduring and of the prospect of a release. I am sure that we can extend to his family and to his friends the sincere condolence and sympathy of every member of this House without exception.

maintopic: DEATH OF MR. JOHN McINTOSH, M.P.
speechtext:
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, as an old colleague of Mr. Mc-Iutosh in the Quebec government, I may be permitted to add my humble testimony to the eloquent tributes which have just been pronounced by my rigid hon. friend, the Prime Minister, and the hon. leader of the opposition, upon the passing of the hon. member for Sherbrooke, one of the most esteemed members of this House. His death, although not quite unexpected, still came as a shock, not only to his friends on this side of the House, but, I am sure, to the members on the other side as well.
Mr. McIntosh was first returned to the legislature of the province of Quebec in 1886. In 1890 he came back before his constituents, and owing to his popularity, victory did not desert him, although the Conservative party were then struggling under very trying circumstances. As a matter of fact. Mr. Mercier had so endeared [DOT]himself to the hearts of the people that it was no easy task for his opponents to secure a fav-vourable verdict. But as Mr. McIntosh had won the confidence and the esteem not only of the people of Sherbrooke, but of every class of the community in the eastern townships, he succeeded in overcoming those difficulties. In 1892, Mr. de Boucherville [DOT]having been entrusted with the responsibility of forming a cabinet, Mr. McIntosh was invited to enter the administration ; and later on, ^hen the Taillon government succeeded that of Mr. de Boucherville, our late lamented colleague was again asked to become a member of the administration. In the various positions w'hicli he has filled, whether as a member of the Quebec legislature or as a member of the government of that province, it may truly be said that [DOT]his never-tiring industry and his ideal devotion to the common weal never faltered. He w-as also chosen as a representative of our province at the great Chicago fair, and there also he discharged his duties in such a manner as to elicit universal praise. The many regrets caused by the lamented death of Mr. McIntosh are not circumscribed to the eastern townships, but I am warranted In saying that they are shared by the whole province of Quebec.
1 join heartily in the kind words uttered by my right hon. friend, the Prime Minister and by the hon. leader of the opposition, and I voice the feelings of sorrow caused on both sides of Che House by the death of so highly esteemed a colleague.

maintopic: DEATH OF MR. JOHN McINTOSH, M.P.
speechtext:
May I be permitted to add a word to what has been so eloquently said by the leader of the govern-

ment, and by the leader of the opposition, on this sad occasion. The late Mr. McIntosh entered public life as the representative of the county which I now have the honour to represent in this House. I knew him personally for many years, and I can say that he wa's an honest and noble-hearted man, who possessed to a remarkable degree the confidence of all nationalities and of all political parties Jn the eastern townships. Beloved by those who knew him most intimately and respected by all in that section of the country, his public and private life will long be remembered as worthy of emulation by those who follow him.

Casgrain) may rest assured that the department has in no way authorized a departure from the proper procedure which would insure that an English form should be given to an English patron of the post office, and a French form to a French patron. I have received a communication to the effect that the young men who have come here to learn musketry are being taxed for the maintenance of clubs, for the maintenance of an extra mess, and for extra furnishings generally. I am also informed that privates are called upon to act as servants to officers, and that these young men who are brought from the farms to learn musketry are subjected to prison discipline. They cannot leave the camp grounds unless they get a pass and they must be in at a certain hour in the evening or they are disciplined. I am told that a number of officers and men were informed that they need not bring extra clothing or bedding, but that they had to purchase them here at considerable expense. I do not know whether or not the officer in charge of the musketry school is responsible for this. This officer goes on to say that he thinks the country pays the Cartwright family dearly enough without having the men who come to take the musketry course taxed by this extra expense. I do not think the people of this country want the young gentlemen, privates or officers who come here, to be subject to prison rule. I do not believe that a young man who comes here and chances to be a

private, should give up one hour of his time to act as servant to any officer, nor do I think that the country should pay these men to act as officers' servants. 1 direct the attention of the minister to these grievances which I believe are founded on fact, and which should be stopped at once. I do not ask him to give any answer to-day, as I have not had time to give him notice that I would bring it up.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: This school of musketry has been in operation for a couple of years, awl this is the first time I have heard any complaint. I was not aware that the system in force this year differed from that of previous years. I am sorry that my: hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) saw fit to make the reference he did to the Cartwright family. I scarcely see what that has to do with it. and I am sure that my hon. friend himself would be the last man to say or to insinuate that any charges that may be imposed on officers attending the school could go into the pocket of as honourable a gentleman as Col. Robert Cartwright is known to be. I am sorry that he made that gratuitous slip. I am very glad, however, that he has called my attention to the fact, and I will make inquiry and be prepared to make a statement on the subject.

My remarks did not directly' or indirectly lead to the inference that one dollar or one farthing of this money went into the pocket of Col. Cartwright, and the minister must have known that. But if the Cartwright family have to be provided for at the public expense, it will have to be done without taxing the officers on the ranges. The minister must not run away with the notion that we are going to bow down to the Cartwright family or any other family in this country.

Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the day are called, I wish to bring to the attention of the House the use made of the press gallery by some journalists. In the ' Mail and Empire ' of yesterday, containing a report sent from this gallery of the discussion on the Militia Bill, I find the following :-
House Discusses the Militia Bill-Mr. Bourassa in Evidence-Objects to Command being
Declared Vested in the King-Displays Militarism Bogey.
Ottawa, July 11.-The Militia Bill was before the House of Commons to-day, and good progress was made in committee. There was a great deal of heated discussion as a result of Mr. Bourassa's opinions on various points proposed. He objected to the command-inchief being declared to be vested in the King. Instead of this, he wanted an amendment declaring it vested in the Governor in Council. This amendment was forced to a vote, and no cne supported Mr. Bourassa.
I never make much effort to gain, I will not say the eulogy, but even the fairness of the Tory press, especially in regard to anything I may say outside of the House ; but as a member of the House, I protest against the use which is made of the privilege granted to journalists who take reports of the debates in this House, in order to send out falsehoods as accurate reports. The House knows very well that this is the exact opposite of what I contended, and of that amendment which I brought before the House. The purpose of that amendment was, on the contrary, to insist on the principle that the command-in-chief of the militia is vested in the King, but that the exercise of that command belongs to the Cana-

diau government. Most of tlie other newspapers of Canada reported it correctly, but the ' Mail and Empire ' took occasion to make such an attack on the amendment and to report the discussion in such a way as to enable that newspaper and the Tory organization of Ontario, I suppose, to say that the member for Labelle wants to cut all ties which unite this country with the United Kingdom. I do not at all mind this accusation, but as a member of the House of Commons, when it is a question of the privilege belonging to the press by virtue of the goodwill of this House, I have not only a right, but I consider it a duty to protest against this kind of reporting being done in the press gallery of this House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Before the motion is put, I would like to bring to the attention of the House some matters referred to in the Auditor General's report for the present year, more especially his suggestion that amendments submitted by him for the consideration of parliament some two or three years ago should be taken into consideration and dealt with without further delay. There is no doubt whatever that the powers and the position of the Auditor General are of great importance to the people of this country. He is the officer of parliament more especially, and it is for members of parliament on both sides of the House, irrespective of party, to consider fairly and impartially any suggestions made by him as to desirable amendments of the Audit Act, for the purpose of enabling him more thoroughly to safeguard the interests of the country and more effectively to protect the public treasury. Whatever opinion may be entertained as to Mr. McDougall's reasonableness or unreasonableness in regard to certain matters which have been before parliament in the past, I think every one will credit him with the desire and intention of performing his duty fearlessly and impartially. He was appointed by the government of Mr. Mackenzie in 1877 or 1878. When the succeeding administration of Sir John A. Macdonald came into power, he was of course retained in office, and I
believe that so far as Sir John A. Macdonald as Prime Minister of this country had the power to support Mr. McDougall in the performance of his duties, he was always found ready to do so, and was always prompt to recognize liis work, his courage and his fidelity as a public officer. Since the present administration came into power there seems to have been more friction between Mr. McDougall and the public departments than formerly prevailed. It is in the very nature of things that some friction should prevail between the Auditor and those departments of the government which he is called upon to check.
I do not at all place out of sight the fact that under preceding administrations Mr. McDougall was occasionally over-ruled and that a certain amount of friction may sometimes have been occasioned by his attitude with regard to certain public expenditure. I have not studied the history of the past so as to know to what extent that did prevail, but no doubt it did prevail to some extent. Since the present administration came into power, that friction seems to have increased, and it has reached its culmination at present, when the Auditor General has, after having given warning on more than one occasion tendered his resignation on the ground that his usefulness as a public ^officer is gone. He gives two .reasons why his usefulness has gone. One is that he is very frequently overruled by the Treasury Board, and the next is that he does not consider the Consolidated Revenue Act in its present condition sufficient for the purposes of his department. The subject was brought up by him, I think in 1899, and in his report dated the 9th of March, 1904, he uses this language :
The following rather lengthy correspondence is introduced in this place because it illustrates the practical importance of several amendments that this office has been asking for some years to have made to the Audit Act.
The amendments to provide : 1st. That no contract with the government be made after the work is completed ; 2nd. That in contracts given without tenders, or. where tenders have been called for and the lotvest tender has not been accepted, the proper officer of the department be required to certify that the prices are fair and just ; 3rd. That in all cases the technical officer on whose expert knowledge the department relied whe'n making the contract, he required to supply the fullest information to the Auditor Generali and all other government officials who have the duty of dealing w'ith contracts.
Further on in the same report he says
The magnitude and number of the transactions going through this office are now so increased that I feel parliament should seriously consider also the amendment of the Audit Act along the other lines suggested in a former report, to enable this office to cope with the expansion of the business of the country. I febl so strongly on this point that

if parliament does not see its way to bring the matter up this session, I shall at the end of the session ask to be superannuated.
Mr. McDougall is an officer of parliament. We are obliged, I think, to look at his recommendations to parliament as those of an impartial officer who has no end to serve other than to perform his duty. Therefore, the Auditor General's suggestions should commend themselves to parliament for consideration and for such action as may seem wise along the lines suggested.
There was a motion earlier in the session by the hon,. member for South Sirncoe (Mr. Lennox), which pointed out the advisability of having the whole question referred to a committee of the House for inquiry and report. That motion was not acceded to by the government, and I now propose to make some suggestions as to certain matters which I think ought to be dealt with at once ; and in making these suggestions, I shall conclude with a motion pointing out in general terms the necessity of making some amendments to the Act. And because my motion mqst necessarily be couched in general terms, I shall take occasion to indicate the matters in respect of which I think the Audit Act might profitably be amended.
In the first place, let me say that the Auditor General has dealt in his report with the so-called Davis contract for the lighting of the Cornwall canal. I do not propose at this moment to deal with that question as I shall deal with it later on when the House is in committee, and when there will be better opportunity of discussing it. But let me call attention to one or two sentences which the Auditor General has used with regard to that contract, In a letter of the 7th July, 1902, Mr. McDougall uses this language in addressing the Secretary of the Treasury Board :
Then I may call your attention to the. rather singular fact that there were two arrangements in connection with the matter. The first was made eleven days before the election of June 23, 1896, and the second twenty-nine days before that of November 7, 1900.
There is a suggestion in that which has been interpreted in a certain way by a portion of the public press, and I desire to point out that the Auditor General has not been quite so accurate in his dates as possibly he might have been expected to be. I am not saying this by way of reproach, but desire to call attention to the actual dates in order that any misapprehension which has been disseminated by the press should be removed. Let me say that in the documents brought down there is an agreement of the 25th of June, 1896, made between the government and Mr. Davis, in which reference is made to certain Orders in Council, dated respectively 18th #f February. 1S9C, and 12th of June, 1896. In order that the Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
true position may be laid before the country, I shall read those Orders in Council. I did not obtain them until yesterday, although I made application more than a week ago. But Mr. Schreiber informed me that on account of the pressing engagements of the clerical staff of the Railways and Canals Department, he could not possibly hand them to me until Monday morning. The first Order in Couucil is as follows :-
On a memorandum dated 8th February. 1896, from the Minister of Railways and Canals, recommending that authority be given to lease to Mr. Michael P. Davis of Ottawa, Ontario, a certain lot of land belonging to the Cornwall canal containing by admeasurement 4-88 acres, be the same more or less, and more particularly described as follows:-
All that piece or parcel of land being part of lot No. 1 at the lower end of Sheik's Island, in the township of Cornwall, in the county of Stormont and province of Ontario ;
Commencing at a point 123 feet in a southeasterly direction from the centre line of the entrance channel to the regulating weir and at right angles thereto and in line with the extreme lower end of the sidewalls of the weir; thence southeasterly on a prolongation of the last course 530 feet, more or less, to the water's edge of the River St. Lawrence; ihence northerly following the water's edge to a line parallel to and seventy feet distant from the centre line of the roadway on the lower Sheik's Island Dam; thence westerly along said parallel line 240 feet more or less to its intersection with a line parallel to and 125 feet distant from the centre line of the entrance channel to the regulating weir ; thence southerly along said parallel line 490 feet more or less to the post planted at the southwesterly angle of the land described; containing by admeasurement 4'88 acres, be the same more or less, and as shown on the sketch plan hereunto annexed, coloured red:-together with so much of the surplus water, if any on Lock No. 20 level, Cornwall canal, as the Minister of Railways and Canals may deem advisable, after navigation and existing mills and mill sites hereinafter to be leased are supplied, the lessee also to have the privilege of using at a weir to be hereafter constructed by him the water flowing into the said canal from Hoople's creek, the said lot of land and the said surplus water and flow of water from Hoople's Creek to be held for the erection of an electric plant and the operation of the machinery therein for the term of twenty one years from and after the first day of July, 1896, and ended on the 1st day of July, 1917, and thereafter for a term of twenty-one years renewable, at a rental of one thousand dollars per annum payable in advance upon the 2nd day of January and the 1st day of July in each year, dating from the first day of July, 1896, the rent for the first two years not being charged. The lessee to supply electric power for the working of all the locks on the Cornwall canal a' sixty-three dollars per horse power per annum, and also electric direct current arc light of not less than 2,000 candle power at thirty cents per light per night, as set forth in the indenture of lease hereto, annexed-
The minister further recommends that the said lease of land, surplus water and flow of water, be upon the terms and conditions set forth in the indenture of lease hereunto annexed, which is hereby submitted for approval, and

that he, the minister be authorized to execute the same on behalf of Her Majesty.
The committee submit the above recommendations for Your Excellency's approval.
(Sgd.) JOHN J. McGEE.
Clerk of the Privy Council.
The next Order in Council is one bearing date of 12th of June, 1896, and is as follows:
On a memorandum dated 22nd May,-1896, from the Minister of Railways and Canals, representing that under date the 12th May inst., the chief engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals has furnished an amended plan and description of the parcel of land, 4-88 acres in extent at the Lower Sheik's island dam on the Cornwall Canal Reserve, authority for-the leasing of which to Mr. M. P. Davis was given by Order in Council of the 18th of February last, which also approved of the draft of the proposed lease.
The minister recommends that the plan and description hereto attached be substituted for the plan and description attached to or embodied in the said Order in Council, and that the draft of lease approved thereby be amended to the effect of such substitution.
The committee submit the same' for your Excellency's approval.
(Sgd.) JOHN J. McGEE, Clerk of the Privy Council.
What I desire to draw to the. attention of the House and the country is this : If dates are of importance in considering this contract, it is especially of importance to note that the Order in Council upon which that agreement was made bears date of 18th February, and not of 12th June. The only effect of the additional Order in Council of June 12th is to provide a new plan and description of the lease which had been approved as far back as 22nd February ; and it is further to be noted that the new Order in Council of 12th June was made upon a memorandum dated 22nd May, from the Minister of Railways and Canals. Therefore, the Order in Council upon which this agreement was made is of date 18th February, 1896, except in so far as the description was slightly amended upon a memorandum dated 22nd May, 1896, confirmed by Order in Council of 12th June, 1896.
Now, the one difficulty which the Auditor General has experienced, as he telis us, in dealing with matters touching public contracts and affecting the expenditure of public money, is that he has no power, where overruled by the Treasury Board to prevent the expenditure of money even though the circumstances attending the making or modification of the contract and the payment of the money are such as, in his opinion, should demand the fullest possible investigation. And the criticisms which have been made upon the report which he has presented to parliament and the country point to the possibility that the two political parties may be so concerned in a matter of public expenditure that neither the 209
one nor the other would press for an investigation by parliament. Now, it is better, when suggestions of that kind are made, either impliedly by the Auditor General or openly in the public press, that some power should be given to the Auditor General or some other officer by means of which that investigation can certainly be instituted and carried on without regard to the interests that might be affected. It is for that reason that I am suggesting to the government to approve of a Bill, a copy of which I have already handed to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick). This Bill I suggest not as one which is to be followed ipsissimis verbis, but as one setting forth a principle, an idea, which, I think, might be safely acted upon by the government, and which would tend to produce in the minds of the people greater confidence in the powers of the Auditor General and in the safeguarding of the public treasury. I will read the draft Bill to which I have referred and make a few comments on it as I proceed :
An Act to amend the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, and the Acts in amendment thereof.
His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows :
1.	The Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act. chapter 29 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, as amended by 51 Victoria, chapter 7, 54-55 Victoria, chapter 16, and 57-58 Victoria, chapter 19, is hereby further amended, by adding thereto the following as section 58 (a) immediately after section 58.
58 (a) (1) In case any contract involving the expenditure of public money has been entered into or modified, or in case any public moneys are about to be paid or have been'paid under the order of the Treasury Board after refusal by the Auditor General to certify to a cheque therefor, and in case the Auditor General is of opinion that the making or modification of such a contract, or the payment or proposed payment of such moneys was not, or is not in the public interest and that the circumstances attending the same require investigation, he may file with the registrar of the Exchequer Court of Canada a petition addressed to the judge of the said court praying that the making or modification of such contract, or the payment , or proposed payment of such moneys and all circumstances relating to, connected with or attending the same may be investigated by the saiid judge who shall thereupon proceed to investigate the same with all convenient speed, first giving due notice of the time and place of such investigation to the Attorney General of Canada and to all other persons interested. Every person so notified shall be at liberty to attend and be heard upon such investigation. The Auditor General shall attend and may be represented by counsel upon such investigation. The said judge at the conclusion thereof shall file his report upon the matters aforesaid with the Auditor General and the same shall be included in the next annual report of the Auditor General and laid before the House of Commons for such action thereon as parliament may deem necessary.



That is a 'provision which should be acted upon by the Auditor General only under very grave circumstances. It is a very large power to give him, but it is a power which, perhaps, might be given him with safety. If he is of opinion that a public contract has been entered into, or-what is more important-has been modified in the interest altogether of the contracting parties, not in the interest of the public, or if he believes that the payment of public moneys has been made, -or is about to be made, under such circumstances as demand careful investigation, then he is at liberty under such grave conditions to file his petition with the judge of the Exchequer Court and have that investigation which he deems necessary, irrespective altogether of the action which either political party or both parties may take in parliament with regard to the matter. The second subsection of this proposed section, is as follows :
(2) Upon the filing of such petition by the Auditor General notice thereof shall forthwith be given to the Minister of Finance by [DOT]the registrar of the said court and except with the written consent and approval of the Auditor General no payment under any such contract so made or modified or under any such order of the Treasury Board shall thereafter be made until after the conclusion of such investigation and until thirty days after the report of the judge shall have been laid before Parliament.
Provided always that whenever it shall appear to the judge that the exigency of public interest requires that some part or the whole of such a payment shall be made before the,conclusion of the investigation or before the expiration of the said period of thirty days, the judge may authorize such payment in whole or in part, and the same may be made accordingly.	,
That is a very important provision, and it should be acted upon of course by the Auditor General only under grave circumstances, and where he thought the facts were sufficiently serious to justify him in so doing. It would enable him to stay the payment under such contract or modified contract, or under any overruling of the Treasury Board, until the matter had been thoroughly investigated before a judge of the Exchequer Court, and until his report had been laid before parliament for action. It is a very important step, I admit, to pass legislation of that kind ; although I must call the attention of the House to the modification which has been embodied in the draft I submit. It is that the judge of the Exchequer Court shall always have power, under such conditions where in his opinion the exigency of the public service demands it, to permit the payments to proceed, even although the Auditor General still withholds his consent. Now I admit fully that we must look at this question from every standpoint, and while I think the principle which I am contending for in this clause is a correct one, I have an open mind as to

the means by which and the limitations under wffiich that principle shall be carried out. On the one hand, we have to consider the safe-guarding of the treasury and the protection of the public interest ; on the other hand, we are not to put arbitrary power into the hands of any one man, even an Auditor General, which will prevent men who enter into contracts with the government from receiving: from banking and other financial institutions that credit which they have been receiving in the past, and which is absolutely necessary if there is to be that competition in the performance of public works which is eminently desirable in the public interest. There is an idea in that section which may require to be modified, but there is an idea which I think might safely be embodied in some such language as that which I have suggested. The third sub-paragraph is as follows :
3. No payment under an order of the Treasury Board authorizing the issue of a cheque which the Auditor General has refused to certify shall be made until ten days after such order has been made and a copy thereof, with the accompanying reasons, delivered to the Auditor General by the secretary of the said board.
The idea is that after the Treasury Board has overruled a refusal of the Auditor General to certify a cheque for expenditure out of the consolidated revenue fund, the Auditor General shall have a certain period within which he shall determine whether it is desirable for him to undertake such an investigation as that which has been provided for in the first subsection of section 1 which I have drafted. Then my draft Bill proceeds as follows :
4 The judge. may examine any person on oath or affirmation on any matter pertinent to such investigation, and may cause a subpoena to be issued from the Exchequer Court commanding any person therein named to appear before him and to testify to all matters within his knowledge relative to the matter under investigation, and to bring with him and produce any document, paper or other thing which he has in his possession relative to the matter under investigation and reasonable travelling expenses shall be tendered to any witness so subpoenaed at the time of service.
5.	If for any reason the judge deems it advisable he may issue a commission for the purposes of such investigation in like manner and with the like powers as are set forth in section 57 of the ' Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act,' with regard to examinations by the Auditor General, and the provisions of sections 57 and 58 of the said Act shall apply to such investigation and to the persons summoned for the purposes thereof. *
6.	The judge shall in all matters relating to such investigation have all the powers and authority of the Court of Exchequer with regard to matters within the jurisdiction of said court.
7.	The procedure and rules of the Exchequer Court so far as applicable shall apply

to such investigation and the judge of the said court may from time to time make, subject to the approval of the Governor in Council, such further or other general rules with regard to such investigations as he may deem necessary.
8.	The provisions of the preceding sevep subsections of this section shall apply to all contracts, payments and matters referred to, or reported upon by the Auditor General in his report for the fiscal year ending 30th day of June, 1903.	| (/j
I have Inserted that special provision because of the suggestion of the Auditor General to which I have, already referred, a suggestion to which I called the attention of the, House. He is mistaken as to the dates.' This contract was entered into, as he says, eleven days, but upon an Order in Council made some four months before the general election of 1896, and the auxiliary contract, if I may so term it, was entered into also shortly before the general election of 1900. There is a suggestion in that which, as I have already said, has been the subject of some criticism, and for that reason I propose to make the provisions to which I have already referred apply not only to the future but also to all matters which are reported upon or dealt with by the Auditor General in his report for the year 1903. That provision gives ample power to thoroughly investigate the Davis contract.
I will now read section 2 of the proposed Bill :
2.	Section 32, subsection 1 of the said Act as amended by the Act 51 Victoria, chapter 7, section 5, is further amended by adding thereto the following as subclause (d) immediately after subclause (c) thereof :-
(d.) The members of the Treasury Board shall furnish reasons for their decision, which reasons shall form part of or be attached to the written order of the board.
I do not think that this is an unreasonable requirement on the part of the Auditor General ; indeed it is necessary for his guidance in the future. If he has so misconceived his powers or duties as auditor as to refuse the payment of public moneys under circumstances which call for the intervention of the Treasury Board, then it is right, not only for the information of the public, but also for his own guidance and his own consideration in the future, that the reasons which have impelled the Treasury Board to overrule him in that regard should be stated to him and reported by him to Parliament.
The third section of my draft Bill is as follows :
3.	Section 48 of the said Act as amended by the Act 51 Victoria, chapter 7, section 10, is hereby repealed and the following substituted therefor
(48.) In reporting as hereinbefore directed for the information of the House of Corn-2094
mons, the result of the examination of the appropriation accounts, the Auditor General shall call attention to every one in which cheques have been issued without his certificate-or in which a grant has been exceeded-or in which money received by a department from other sources than the grants for the year to which the account relates has not been applied or accounted for according to the directions of parliament-or in which a sum charged against a grant is not supported by proof of payment-or in which a payment so charged did not occur within the period of the account, or was for any other reason, not properly chargeable against the grant, or was in any way irregular,-
So far the statute proceeds exactly as it is at the present time. What I am reading further is new. My proposed amendment continues as follows :
-or in which a sum charged against a grant for capital account was expended wholly or in part for a purpose properly chargeable to revenue account, or in which by reason pf the generality of the appropriation, or otherwise, he has been unable to properly check or control the expenditure, or to confine it to what he believes to have been the abject of the House of Commons in making the grant.
It seems to me that these are matters in respect to which the Auditor General should report to parliament, because they are matters of importance, and it is well that parliament should be informed as to irregularities or defects of that kind.
The fourth section of the Bill which I have drafted is as follows :
Section 21 of the said Act as amended by 51 Victoria, chapter 7, section 1, is further amended by striking out the words ' four thousand ' and substituting therefor the words.
I have left a blank here so as to suggest an increase in the salary of the Auditor General.^ His salary at the present time I believe is $4,000, and it has continued at that sum for a long period of time. As deputy ministers and others have had their salaries increased within recent years, and as the cost of living has undoubtedly increased during that period, and as the Auditor General is an old and a faithful public servant, it seems to me it would not be out of place at the present time to give him some further consideration in the way of a salary, and it is for that purpose I have drawn section 4 of the Bill in its present form, leaving of course for the consideration of the government and of parliament what should be the increase to his salary.
Before sitting down I would like to say a few words about the suggested Audit Act which was submitted to parliament with the report of the Auditor General some three or four years ago. In the first place the Auditor General suggests that his title should be changed to , ' The Controller and Auditor General of Canada.' That is not a matter perhaps of very great importance and for my part I see no reason why the title

should not be so changed; it is more of form than of substance.
The first important change that I observe in the suggested Audit Act proposed by the Auditor General is that in section 24 he suggests an omission which gives to him, uncontrolled by the Treasury Board, the power to make orders and rules for the conduct of the internal business of his office. For my own part I would regard that as a reasonable request. I think we might safely trust to the Auditor General the power to make rules for the internal business of his office.
The next matter of importance, if it is of importance, is his suggestion that the account to which all public moneys, from whatever source of revenue derived are paid in, should be called 'the Canadian Exchequer Account,' instead of the ' account of the Minister of Finance and Receiver General.' In regard to this the Auditor General expresses his views as follows :
It is important that the public should understand clearly that the money is not in any way the money of the government until after it has been provided by parliament.
Therefore the Auditor General suggests that the account, instead of being called ' the account of the Minister of Finance and Receiver General,' should be called ' the Canadian Exchequer Account.' and in that change he says we will be following the example of the Imperial Audit Act. That however I do not regard as of so much importance as the amendment which he suggests with regard to section 30.
Section 30 is altered very much in the form which he has suggested. The most important amendment it seems to me which he has proposed is that he desires credits to be issued in favour of the deputy head, an accountant of a department, or to two, officers, clerks or other persons, connected with the office or service charged; As I understand it the credit here referred to might be spoken of as the petty cash service of each department. Of course very large sums actually are paid out of that account but relatively speaking, it is. as it were, the petty cash service of eaeh department A credit is made at the request of the Auditor General, by the Minister of Finance and Receiver General in favour of each department and out of that credit moneys are paid for certain public services and in the end the moneys' so paid out of that credit are audited and checked by the Auditor General. He suggests that these credits should be made to the deputy and the accountant of each department, or to at least two officers of the department and I think that would be a desirable amendment.
He makes a further suggestion which is also of importance. He suggests that:
No such credit shall issue in favour of any officers or other persons in excess of Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
(the) appropriations authorized (and assigned as above, or when, in using previous credits, the applicants have disobeyed an Act of parliament or other valid regulations).
He suggests also :
These credits shall he used only for such class or classes of payments as the Controller and Auditor General may direct.
And further :
If the Controller and Auditor General notify one of the persons in whose names a credit has been issued, that such credit is not to be used for any specified purpose, such credit shall not he used for such purpose, but for any payment to be made for such purpose a cheque on the Canada Exchequer Account shall be applied for.
I understand the reason for his proposal is this :	Under the present Act where the
Auditor General has made a credit which is available for the use of a public department, he may afterwards find that under some contract, or under some modified contract, a payment is proposed which he feels he could not sanction, and he may go to the officers of the department possessing that credit and express his views in that regard. But they are entirely at liberty to disregard his views ; they may continue to make payments of which he expressly disapxiroves out of these credits, leaving him only the opportunity of criticising after the payments have been made instead of objecting and withholding the payments, as he otherwise might do. I would be inclined to think that the two suggestions on this line are well worthy of consideration by this House, and I do not see that the administration of public affairs would be in any way hampered by complying with the desire of the Auditor General in this respect.
I frankly and fully admit that in dealing with the suggestions of the Auditor General we must have in mind always the fact that there is ministerial responsibility for public expenditure and we must also bear in mind the fact that we must uot so hamper the administration of public affairs that it cannot be carried on efficiently; but, subject to those two qualifications, it seems to me that we ought to place in the hands of the Auditor General all possible safeguards for the protection of the public interest and the public money.
I may say very frankly that I would not be inclined to assent to some of the suggestions which the Auditor General has made as to section 33 without further explanation and a better understanding of how they could be fairly and properly carried out having regard to the considerations which I have mentioned, but there are two suggestions with regard to section 33 which I think might well be taken into consideration by the government. One of these suggestions is :

If an official of any department, dealing with a claim against the government, knows that the claimant is indebted to the government, whether the indebtedness is of record in the department or not, he shall take no part in the payment of the claim against the government, except to the extent that the amount dpe by the government exceeds that due to it.
The principle of this proposed amendment seems to be a very proper one, although possibly the language of the Auditor General might require modification in order to carry out his idea.
Another suggestion made by the Auditor General is in reference to section 37 :
The Controller and Auditor General may require the production of any public document connected with any expenditure which is before him for examination.
At present I do not see that there can possibly be any objection to his having that power ; in fact it would seem to me that in the public interest he ought to have that power. Some of these suggestions that he has made with regard to section 33 would seem to me to interfere with the theory of ministerial responsibility and with the efficiency of the public administration and would rather place the Auditor General in the position of a Court of Appeal from the administration in respect to matters which must be absolutely entrusted to them under our system of responsible government. Therefore, without more fully understanding what exactly is meant or required by the Auditor General in making these propositions, I would not be inclined to support him with regard to them.
Another suggestion which he has made which seems to be worthy of consideration is in reference to section 47. Section 47 is as follows :
If, during the progress of the examination by the Controller and Auditor General hereinbefore directed, any objection arises to any item to be introduced into the appropriation account of any grant, such objections shall, notwithstanding such account has not been rendered to him, be immediately communicated to the department concerned ; and it the objections are not answered to his satisfaction by such department

The statute at present continues as follows :
-they shall be referred by him to the Treasury Board, and the Treasury Board shall determine in what manner the items in question shall be entered in the annual appropriation account.
The Auditor General's suggestion is that it should read as follows instead of the language which*! have just read :
And if the objections are not answered to his satisfaction by such department he shall disallow the item, or make such change as appears to him proper.
I would be inclined to think that the suggestion of the Auditor General in this regard is a wise one and that there is no good reason in the public interest why that suggestion should not be acted upon.
I think these are all the suggestions of the Auditor General that I find necessary to call attention to at present. It seems to me that the subject is worthy the immediate consideration of the government. I regret that the government did not see fit, at an earlier stage of the session to submit the whole question to this House for the purpose of enabling us to give to it that consideration which we cannot give to it now, and which would probably have been productive of better results than we may hope for at- this late period. For the purpose of bringing the matter before the House, and not in any way as a motion of want of confidence in the government, but in order that a discussion may arise on the whole subject, I beg to move :
That all the words after the word ' that ' in the main motion be left out, and the following substituted therfefor :-
In the opinion of this House the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act should be so extended as to confer upon the Auditor General powers ample in every respect to protect the public interest and to safeguard the public treasury.
That resolution must necessarily be general, because I cannot very well introduce the provisions of an Act of parliament into a resolution. I have submitted to the House my views in regard to the amendments which ought to be made, and whether they are made or not they are at least entitled to the earnest and careful consideration of this House before they should be disregarded.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The leader of the opposition has moved an amendment which expresses an abstract opinion, and which perhaps would have had no very definite meaning, if my hon. friend had not in his remarks associated with his motion certain proposed amendments to the Audit Act. It is therefore our duty to deal with the amendment in which he proposes to express the opinion of the House ; that the consolidated Revenue and Audit Act should be so extended as to confer upon the Auditor General powers ample in every respect to protect the public interest and safeguard the public treasury. From my own point of view I am unable to vote for that motion inasmuch as it implies that the existing powers are not sufficient for the purpose. I differ entirely from the Auditor General, I differ entirely from my hon. friend if he agrees with the Auditor General, when he implies that the powers of the Audit Act are not at this moment ample and sufficient for the protection of the public treasury. The principles un-

defying the Audit Act were established long years ago under certain conditions, and the conditions existing now are precisely the same as they were then. The volume of business has increased, but that simply means that you have to give to the Auditor General a large staff to do his work. There are no new principles ; no new difficulties, nothing has occurred in the administration of the Audit Act under the present government that has not occurred frequently under the administration of all other governments. Therefore, the suggestion that some need has arisen for a new provision in the Audit Act, is a proposition to which I am unable to give my assent. I do not quite understand what the leader of the opposition meant when he [DOT] said that he regretted that the government had not seen lit at an earlier stage of the session to submit this whole matter to the House. In what manner could we have submitted this matter to the whole House ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I referred to the motion for a committee to investigate the whole question of the Audit Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That motion was made by my hon. friend from Sirncoe (Mr Lennox) and the leader of the opposition regrets that it was not acceded to by the government. I think he might have added that that motion was not acceded to by the opposition, because I think I am correct In stating that when the time came to divide the House on that motion there were not a dozen members present on the opposition side, and several of these had remained for the purpose of voting against the motion. The motion was not even pressed to a division, so that when my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) complained that it was not acceded to by the government he hardly puts the case fairly. The motion to which he refers was practically condemned by both sides of the House as something, if not uncalled for, certainly as something that did not commend itself to the judgment of the House. There is no difficulty about the Auditor General having the most full and ample power to investigate. From the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) one might assume that there was some difficulty in regard to the Auditor General's power to make inquiry. There is absolutely none. Under the Audit Act at present, the Auditqr General is properly vested with large powers ; unlimited powers to investigate everything in connection with the public accounts. He has unlimited power to, audit ; he lias even the power to obstruct, which was never the intention of the Audit Act at all. There is no lack of power to the Auditor General in the Audit Act, and if our friend the Auditor General wants more power, it is not that he may audit the public accounts, but that he may ' Mr. FIELDING.	'
deal with matters which the Audit Act never contemplated as coming within the proper sphere of the Auditor General's duty. I join with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition in giving credit to the Auditor General for what he believes to be a faithful discharge of his duties. The nature of the Auditor General's business makes him critical ; hypercritical, suspicious, sensitive. He is somewhat like a police officer in a court of law whose zeal for conviction is so strong that-the judges look upon his evidence with a degree of doubt and always discount It a little. The Auditor General, by the very nature of his business falls into an atmosphere of suspicion, and he sometimes sees difficulties where none exist. I do not say that as against Mr. Mc-Dougall, but I say it as a condition which is likely to arise out of the very nature of his work ; and so very often we have the Auditor General raising questions which are not questions of audit, but which are questions of public policy. My hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) has associated with his motion suggestions as to certain amendments to the Audit Act. I have never had the pleasure of seeing them or hearing them until they were read in the House to-day, and it would not be wise for anybody to reach conclusive opinions from a very hasty knowledge of a matter of such importance.
I do not anticipate that at this stage of the session we would; be able to give that subject the grave consideration which it ought , to receive if we were to undertake to deal with it. My hon. friend has remarked that the Auditor General, is in a particular manner the servant of parliament. That is true, and that indicates that in a particular manner every member of parliament perhaps has a little larger responsibility in dealing with the affairs of the" Auditor General, than in dealing with the affairs of the ordinary government official. The leader of the opposition has reminded us that as far back as 1899 the Auditor General began to make complaints as to the need of amendments to the Audit Act, and he has read from a more recent report several changes which the Auditor General desires. My hon. friends opposite have therefore had the Auditor General's views before theih for three or four years, and I am bound to believe that if they thought there was any good ground for complaint and any real need of amendments to the Audit Act in the public interest, they would have brought them forward before this, and not waited until the last stages of this session to come forward with an abstract motion simply stating that we need larger powers for the Auditor General. I do no1* think the hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) has established any case for a change, but certainly before we could undertake to make the change which he has suggested, the House

would have to very carefully consider its position. Without following my hon. friend closely through the proposed amendments which he read, one fact comes out straight and clear, and that is that the control of the expenditure of public money is to be taken from the people's parliament and given to the judge of the Exchequer Court. That is the essence of the whole proceeding, that is the foundation of the proposed Bill.
It was Sir John Macdonald who on one occasion said that among the many rights which the parliament of Canada possessed, was the right to do wrong, and it was better that parliament should exercise its right to do wrong than that other people should deny parliamentary rights. The principles of parliamentary government are such that we are bound to believe that the people through their representatives will deal with every grievance ; and the attempt to get behind the people's representatives, to create some other tribunal, to take the place of parliament, especially in matters of money, and lo give that body .power independent of the government and parliament to deal wTith these matters, is a step in the wrong direction ; and we on this side of the House are not prepared to take it. We have. no reason to suppose that treasury boards and governments under either party are likely to be composed otherwise than of honourable men. It is not necessary for the purpose of our discussion to assume that on one side or on the other there would not be a desire to protect the public interest. We are bound to assume that men placed in the high position of ministers of the parliament of Canada, though they differ in their political stripe from men across the House, will in the main be honest and conscientious in their desire to protect the public interests ; and any assumption that on the part of the government or the Treasury Board, and still more by collusion and bargain with hon. gentlemen opposite, there is to be suppression of truth and justice and violation of the public interests, is something that we say this parliament could not assent to, but is something that hon. members on both sides should resent, whether It comes from the Auditor General or anybody else.
On the general questions involved I do not wish to say any more ; but I would like to say a word or two in regard to what is called the Davis contract, to which my hon. friend has referred in the course of his remarks. I will deal with it only generally, because I have not charged my mind with the details. There is a very erroneous impression conveyed to the public as to the action of the Auditor General on that subject. The claim of Mr. Davis arose out of a series of contracts, one beginning in 1896. Some point is made of a difference of a few days in dates in 189C. I do not suppose a few days are more important in
1 189G than they are in 1900, and we need not dwell on that. A claim was made by | Mr. Davis for moneys alleged to be due under his contract. That claim came before the department. The department reported that the money was due, and applied for a cheque. The Auditor General objected, and then the matter came before the Treasury Board. The Treasury Board inquired into it, and the view they took was this, that whether the contract to which that claim referred was or was not an improvident contract, the claim was one which probably had a foundation of law. We called upon our proper officers to advise us whether or not it was a lawful claim. We were advised that the money was due. Whether or not the contract was wisely made, whether the prices were high or low, whether the quantity of power to be taken was greater or less than it wras prudent to take -all these were legitimate questions to debate at a certain stage, but not at that stage, because we were advised that the money was due. The Treasury Board therefore decided that they were bound, under the advice given them, to overrule the objection of the Auditor General, and that that account, up to the date to which it referred, if it was one which could be collected by process of law, was an account which we were bound to pay. But there was a clause in the original contract made by the hon. member for South Lamrk (Mr. Haggart) in 1896, that the government might acquire possession of all these works of Mr. Davis. In that clause there was an opportunity for a remedy if the contract was found to be an improvident one ; and the Treasury Board took the view that though we would be obliged to pay Mr. Davis's claim up to the date to which he had rendered his account, whether we should continue to do so thereafter was a proper matter for inquiry. That was the position of the matter then. The Treasury Board were not called on to decide whether or not it was an improvident contract. What they were called on to consider was whether or not Mr. Davis's claim was legally and properly due ; and, after legal advice, the accuracy of which has never been questioned, we decided that the claim would have to be paid. Thereupon the Treasury Board passed a minute overruling the Auditor General and deciding to pay the claim. Before that minute came into effect, before any action was taken upon it, some conversation occurred between some of my colleagues and the Auditor General regarding that claim. Just from whom the suggestion first came I do not know, but the outcome of that conversation was that it was thought better to hold the matter open for a time, and enter into negotiations with Mr. Davis to see if another contract could be made which would be more satisfactory to
