Auditor General.
Mr. McDougall makes it perfectly plain that he is making superannuation the last consideration. His first consideration is that he be provided with such additional means as are necessary under the changed conditions, many of which the ministry have furnished by their own arbitrary action. He asks that these changes be made, and if they are not made he plainly intimates that only one course is left open to him, namely, to retire. Now, I am sorry to see in some very respectable quarters, in some sections of the press supporting the government of the day, some comments which I think are very unfair. X am sorry to see that they have taken their cue from the Minister of Finance, and they speak of the Auditor General as a gentleman to be looked upon with great suspicion, that he is a meddlesome person, that he would be dishonest himself if he had an opportunity. Let me read from a very respectable newspaper supporting the hon. gentlemen opposite some comments upon the conduct of the Auditor General since his resignation became public, and I will leave it to the hon. gentlemen opposite to judge whether this is an honest criticism, whether it is a criticism that they share in. If they do share in it, I am sure nobody will be disposed to dispute their sole possession of it. This is only one of the many extracts that I might quote from different newspapers. The Sarnia ' Observer,' a I.iberal newspaper, had this to say in its issue of June 28, 1904. Its heading ' The watchdog is willing, ' is very significant in view of the article which follows :
The ' watch dog of the treasury,' as the Auditor General is sometimes designated, shows in his application for superannuation that he is as ready to raid the treasury when he sees a chance as any one of those whom he has been taxing in his annual reports with making demands that were not Justified by the services performed. He states in his application that he will accept superannuation if the government will add ten years to the length of his service. This is to be done so that he may receive a larger superannuation allowance than his real services entitle him to. He is asking the government to commit an illegal act so that he may draw out of the treasury for the balance of his life more Mr. CLANCY.
money than is fairly and lawfully coming to him-the very thing that the Auditor General is specially charged to guard against. It would be a huge joke on the Auditor General if the government acceded to his request and his successor vetoed the payment of the extra pension money on the ground that it had not been earned, and payment of it would be illegal.
This comment is a very fair specimen of comments that are appearing in Liberal journals supporting this government, a Liberal government that is driving an officer of parliament from his position. I am told that there are some hon. gentlemen sitting in this House who are looking forward to filling the position of Auditor General. I would like to ask what is the position of any man, inside or outside of this House, who may accept that position following upon the course now contemplated by the government of absolutely refusing to do anything. The only disposition which the government has shown is to tie the hands of the chief officer of parliament and not to give him such facilities as he is entitled to and as the people of this country will demand should be afforded to him. The man who next fills that position will have a rule of conduct laid down in advance that he is to be the pliant creature of the government and if he is not such a creature he will not get the appointment. That is written in black and white, and if he does not obey that rule he will know' what is to follow ; he is to be attacked and blackguarded by the Liberal journals of this country, to be told that because he is seeking what a man may seek under an Act of parliament, what men are obtaining every day although they have been servants in less important capacities than the Auditor General, that he is seeking to obtain illegally, money that does belong to him. I do not know whether it has been the rule of the government to starve a chief officer. This man, Mr. McDougall, received some advance in his salary some 16 years ago. There is no position in the service of the government, except that of the Prime Minister, in which a public servant earns so great a salary by services performed, as that of Auditor General. Here is a man receiving a salary which might ordinarily be called a fair salary, but which, by comparison with the salaries paid for other services, is a beggarly salary. Great responsibilities are attached to the position, and where there are great responsibilities you must get good men to fill the positions and must pay salaries commensurate with these responsibilities. If you do not you cannot expect to get the men. If hon. gentlemen lay down the rule that they are going to starve servants they will get men to work as cheaply or more cheaply, but they will be men who wrill be willing to comply with the rules which the government lay down rather than the rules that should be laid down for the guidance of an Auditor Gen-

eral. I know of no case since Mr. McDou-gall has been appointed where a man has been treated in this way, speaking not In a personal but in a broad official sense. This world can, of course, get along without any man, but we cannot get along without healthy principles for the guidance of men in all walks of life. It is not a matter of great personal concern whether the Auditor General goes out of office, but I repeat again, it is a serious question in a broad sense, and one which cannot be put aside with one wave of the hand, in what-I was going to call the undignified-manner adopted this afternoon by the Minister of Finance. I still do not despair that the government will not allow this session to go by without taking steps to put this matter right. I do not know the mind of the Auditor General, but he is a man who has those correct and stern ideas of public duty which would induce him to risk everything at his time of life, at a time when a man may not easily obtain other employment. He has, as I say, put everything aside in the interests of public duty. I am still unwilling to believe that the government will allow his resignation to take place, and I trust that while they may vote down this resolution they will deal with this matter during the present session.

As an admirer of the Auditor General and as one who has a great deal of sympathy and personal friendship for him, I was, in common with a great many people in Canada, shocked at the statements that were made by him in connection with what is known as the Davis contract, which has given rise, I presume, to most of the discussion which has taken place in connection with his desire for a change in his status. I have read carefully the Auditor General's statement in connection with that matter. I did so with considerable interest after seeing in the ' Evening Journal,' in the Toronto ' News ' and in * Saturday Night ' statements of which this is a fair sample :
Credit the Auditor General with a half million saved. The way he butted in. How government contracts sometimes go, especially Just before general elections. The story of the light and power agreement for Cornwall canal. Half a million dollars or more in one contract saved to the public treasury by the interference of the Dominion Auditor General. A bad contract made infinitely worse by a Liberal government ; partially redeeming action taken later by the Laurier administration, hut the worse feature remaining.
And so on. Of course as a member of parliament and one interested in the good name of the government I was exceedingly anxious to see whether the statements contained in that paper were true and I therefore read with considerable care the various documents presented by the Auditor General, and I have come to the conclusion, after a careful reading of his letters and the state-2104
ments that he has made, and the answers made by the government, that the Auditor General was wrong in his dates, wrong in his facts, wrong in his inferences, wrong in his conclusions. It appeared to me that if the Auditor General had been animated by a feeling of hostility to the past government and to the present government he could not possibly have adopted a course more calculated to give vent to such a feeling. _ What was there in the contract of 1896 to justify the construction placed upon it by the Auditor General ? Tin? Auditor General unfortunately put himself in the position, not of an auditor, but of a critic, an adverse critic of the government, animated with the desire to do them all the harm he possibly could. After having shown the tremendous loss that the country was about to sustain in a letter addressed to the Treasury Board he says :
Then I call your attention to the rather singular fact that there were two arrangements in connection with this matter. The first was made eleven days before the election of June 23rd, 1896, and the other twenty-nine days before that of November 5, 1900.
The inference naturally left upon the mind of a person not familiar with all the circumstances was that the late government and the present government had entered into a contract which was exceedingly valuable for the contractor in consequence of a liberal political subscription on his part. Is there anything to justify that ? I regard that statement made by the Auditor General as an insult to the Minister of Railways in 1896 and equally insulting to the members of the government of the present day. What was there in the contract of 1896 to justify the statement that it was inspired and completed eleven days before the election of 1896 whereby the Conservative party would get a liberal political subscription ? Is there anything in the contract to justify the statement ? Are the dates of the Auditor General correct ? He is wrong in both instances. He says here eleven days before the election, and yet to-day the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) said that the Order in Council was signed on February 18, or four months before the election took place, and the contract itself was signed on the 25th, or two days after the time the Auditor General says.
In a matter of such moment dates are of much importance. If this contract were finished up in the interests of the contractor, eleven days before the elections, there might be an inference that there was something crooked in it; but all the Auditor General's statements in connection with that are wrong. The contract was not made eleven days before, but two days after the elections, and the Order in Council was passed four months before. Therefore, the imputation that the Auditor General throws upon the late government that in making this contract they were influenced in order

to get an election subscription from the contractor, is false upon its face. It appears to me that the Auditor General suppresses a significant fact in connection with the late contract. In the light we now have, we may believe that the contract entered into in 1896 was probably improvident, but we have no right to assume that it was corrupt, because there is nothing to indicate a corrupt intention. The government were to pay for a certain number of horsepower at a certain rate, and also for a certain number of lights to be determined on thereafter, at so much per light. It may be that with the knowledge we had of electricity in these days, it was impossible for the government to tell whether the price was too dear or not, but anyhow they put in a clause, that by giving twelve months' notice they could take over this work from the contractor, and that very clause should prevent it from being regarded as a corrupt transaction. If in 1896 they were paying too much for horse-power or light, any subsequent parliament, by giving twelve month's notice, could take the matter out of the hands of the contractor, and under such circumstances I should think a contractor would not be willing to put up a very large sum in order to obtain a contract. The element of corruption is removed by this very clause. But, why did the Auditor General go on to say that the second contract was made twenty-nine days before the election, thus conveying the impression that the contractor was this time giving a liberal contribution to the funds of the Liberal party ; that the Conservative party not then being in a position to advance his interests he flopped over and made it of interest to the present government to increase by 63 years the term of his contract, and to require a larger horsepower and a greater number of lights than were necessary. The contract itself does justify any such statement. We are told by no less a person than the lawyer of the Auditor General, a lawyer selected by himself. that that was not true ; that the present government made no new contract, and that it was their duty to fix the number of lights and the amount of horse-power required according to the contract of 1896. That is all the present government has done. What was there in that transaction to justify the Auditor General pointing out significantly that this contract was entered into twenty-nine days before the election of 1900 ? What was there to justify him in conveying the impression that there was a corrupt intent ? What was there to justify him in conveying the impression to the Liberal electors that the Conservative government was corrupt in 1896, and to the Conservative electors that the Liberal government was corrupt in 1900 ? The contract itself on its face shows that the statement of the Auditor General is incorrect, because he was Mr. HEYD.	_	(
wrong in his dates. It was not made before the election, but after the election, and the Order in Council went out four months before. If the present government did not make a new contract; if they did not increase the advantages to the contractor ; if they simply carried out the terms of the contract of 1S96, what justification have these newspapers for the statement that both governments are corrupt, and that the Auditor General butted in and saved 8500,000 to the people of Canada ? I believe it is the intention of the Auditor General to be honest and to look after the interest and welfare of the country, but like a great many others he leans over too much to one side. There * have been a number of Liberal judges appointed in Ontario during the last few years, but instead of the Liberals being able to get any advantage from them, they lean over to the Conservative side, and in this particular instance the Auditor General being a well known Liberal. I presume he thought it his duty to be particularly careful of his treatment of the Liberal government, lest he might be accused of partiality, and so he has leaned jsver, and wherever there was an opportunity of conveying the impression that there was cerruptness or crookedness, the Auditor General has given special significance to these things, and evidently concealed all the redeeming features in the contract. If the late government made a mistake, and if we are paying too high a price under this contract then on twelve months' notice the work can be taken out of the hands of the contractor at its actual value plus five percent. Under such circumstances there is no necessity for scare headings being used in the newspapers, and it is unjust for them to attribute a corrupt intent to the government. I always had the opinion in days gone by, that contractors for the Conservative government managed things a good deal slicker than is apparently the case here. If there were a clause in every contract allowing the government to take over the work on twelve months' notice, I should think there would be no danger of anybody getting a rake off from contractors. In my opinion the powers given to the Auditor General at the present time are wide enough. I do not profess to be able to bring the knowledge of expert accountants to bear upon the subject, but I have here the opinion of Mr. Aylesworth, a lawyer of great judgment who was asked by the Auditor General to give his opinion, and Mr. Aylesworth gives it, not as a politician, but as one of the most eminent counsels in Canada, and he says :
I cannot find from examining and considering the Audit Act any indication that parliament intended your office to be superior, to, or to exercise any supervision over, the various departments of the government, in so far as questioning the validity of their contracts is concerned, but there appears clear provision

in the statute for bringing all such questions to the notice of parliament itself.
The legislation seems to afford a very complete scheme by which your department may be an efficient check upon expenditure, and by which parliament may be at once informed if anything unusual or irregular takes place. You have the power (and no doubt the duty) under section 32 (c) of the Audit Act, to refuse your certificate if at any time convinced that a cheque is applied for where ' the money is not justly due.' You are by section 33 expressly precluded from authorizing any payment unless upon due voucher that the work has been performed or materials supplied. By section 10 of 51 Victoria, chapter 7 (1888), you are, in reporting to the House, to call attention to every case in which cheques have been issued w'ithout your certificate, or in which a payment was ' in any *way irregular.' Your duty accordingly when not satisfied that money claimed is justly due is to refuse to certify, and thereupon the Treasury Board becomes ' the judge of the sufficiency of your protection.'
But the statute has carefully provided that in all such cases the matter must come before parliament upon full report, making it apparently, by section 49 of the Audit Act, your personal duty to present such report if the Minister of Finance does not do so within the time prescribed by the statute.
Responsibility is by this means removed from you and made to rest upon the proper shoulders. The Treasury Board is responsible to parliament, and if parliament considers that in this matter or in any other matter upon which vou may take a similar course an improvident or improper contract has been entered into, the minister who is responsible, or the government, will be held to account.
He secured the opinion of Mr. Aylesworth, one of the most eminent lawyers in this country, who gave his opinion that the powers that the Auditor General ought to have are amply provided for in the present law. Z am willing, on the present occasion, to take Mr. Aylesworth as my guide, as I have not the functions or the legal knowledge necessary for me to express an opinion. But I say that the Auditor General apparently was wrong in his dates, wrong in his facts, wrong in his conclusions and wrong in his deductions. He appears to have charged the late government, and the present government impliedly, with a corrupt intent, contrary to the very documents themselves ; and, that being so, I am quite content to abide by the opinion of Mr. Aylesworth and the present government, that the Auditor General has at present quite enough power to enable him to efficiently discharge his duties as auditor.

Mr. Speaker, it is rather refreshing to hear the specious arguments to which the hon. gentleman has just treated the House. He starts out by saying That the Auditor General is wrong in his dates, wrong in his facts, wrong in his interpretation, wrong in his conclusions and wrong in his deductions-according to the high authority of the member for Brant
(Mr. Heyd), the one man who has been at the business for a quarter of a century, endeavouring by every means in his power to interpret the law according to his best judgment, and, when he found that his interpretation of the law did not meet with the approval of others, submitting it to the ablest lawyer he could find in the country, and following his advice as far as he believed it to be correct. If there was no other evidence to show that the Auditor General was an honest and conscientious man, it seems to me that very fact is sufficient. The hon. member went on to say that, notwithstanding the fact that the Auditor General had been appointed by the present government, he was found in opposition to them at almost every turn when money was being paid out. When the previous government was in power and the same Auditor General disagreed with them with regard to the payment of public money, his friends proclaimed that as an evidence of bis fairness. The hon. gentleman is doing what he nearly always does ; he makes his statement and then runs out, as if he were doing something sharp. It seems to me that a man wlio makes an argument and cannot listen to the reply is either wanting in moral courage or in courtesy. When the same Auditor General opposed the late government with reference to the payment of money the hon. gentleman's friends held that to be an evidence of his ability and fairness, and an evidence that the government of that day was doing something improper ; but when the same man' comes into contact with his friends and endeavours to guard the public treasury in the same way as he did in the time of their predecessors, he is declared to be a man wanting in judgment, wrong in his facts, wrong in his interpretation, wrong in his conclusions and wrong in his deductions ; and, therefore, he can only do it for a malicious purpose against the very party who put him in office. Is that human nature ? Is that likely ? Will the great mass of the peopl# believe that ? I do not think they will. If there was one thing needed to justify the conclusion that the Auditor General is an honest and conscientious man, it is the very thing we are discussing to-day. This, 1 say, is complimentary to his fairness, to his impartiality, to his honesty of purpose. He is doing faithfully, no matter which party is in power, what ho believes he was put there to do ; that is, to guard the public treasury, and to see that no money is paid out unless it is authorized by parliament, and to see that payments are made in accordance with the provisions made by parliament. The hon. member defends the contract. After reading it and considering it, he comes to the conclusion that the contract for lighting the Cornwall canal and supplying power is a good one, that there is nothing wrong with it, that it is defensible, and he is willing to defend it; and he gives,

not only the present government, but the late government, a certificate of purity and competency in making this contract. What did the Minister of Finance say before dinner ? He said : After going over the contract, we agreed with the Auditor General that it ought to be revised and amended, and we submitted a draft to the Auditor General, so as to be satisfied that it would meet with his approval before we entered into it; it met with his approval, and we withdrew the Order in Council which we had previously passed. Was that not an admission that it was wrong before ? If it was not wrong, was there any necessity to change it ? Is not that the strongest argument that the Auditor General was right ? Some very severe strictures were passed on the Auditor General, because, after the government withdrew the Order in Council and endeavoured to have it go into oblivion, he allowed it to see the light. The hon. member for Brant went on to say that the Auditor General is like some of the judges, too straight-so straight that he leans over the other way. That is a very fine compliment to the judges of the country. Coming from the source it does, it will not perhaps be regarded as of much account. To say that the judges of the country are not impartial, but that they show partiality by leaning too much the other way, is the stricture of one of the parties responsible for their appointment ; and then he turns around and compares the Auditor Genera! with them, saying' that he has a similar nature, that he leans over too far the other way. I assume that the hon. gentleman must have meant ihat he leans towards the Conservative party. The hon. member says'the Auditor General is trying to provide arguments to the Conservative party to enable them to put the government out of power. In that be is unfair. What is the resolution before us ? It is a simple one, and one, in my judgment, justified by the facts which have been brought out from year to year. It is as follows :
That in the opinion of this House the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act should be so extended as to confeT on the Auditor General powers ample in every respect to protect the public interest and to safeguard the public treasury.
That is all it is. If the law to-day does not enable the Auditor General to protect the public interest and safeguard the public treasury, as it was intended by its framers it should do, then we ought to supply what is necessary to make it effective. Every year we have had our attention drawn by the Auditor General to the fact that the ,Act does not provide sufficiently .ample powers. As an evidence that his representations have a solid basis, I can point to the fact that several times the Act has been amended to meet his suggestions. That surely proves that he was right in the representations he made. Well, since the last Mr. SPROULE.
extension of the Act, he has again and again drawn our attention to the fact that other amendments are necessary. Of course as time goes on we find defects in laws which were not anticipated when they were passed. The defects in the Audit Act, the Auditor General has pointed out to parliament, so that parliament may act. We are asked to-day why the Conservative party do not bring in any amendment. What would: be the use ? How many Bills have the Conservative party brought into this House, and how many days have they not spent in trying to get the House to pass these Bills, but all to no avail ? Everybody knows that the very fact that these Bills received the support of the Conservative party was sufficient reason to bon. gentlemen opposite to vote them down. And the same fate would overtake any amendment to the Audit Act which we might propose from this side. The government would not allow any amendment proposed by the opposition to pass, because that would be a reflection on themselves. The Minister of Finance says that the Act gives the Auditor General ample powers in every respect. But if it does, bow comes it that three or four years ago the Public Accounts Committee considered this question at great length and decided that the Act was not sufficiently ample ? The ex-Minister of Finance, Mr. Foster, was on that committee and also the present Finance Minister, and that committee decided that it was necessary to give additional power to the Auditor General. Why then was that not done? It was not done because the session was short and coming to its close, and there was not time to consider what measure might be advised. At various times since the matter has been brought up in the Public Accounts Committee, but no remedy has been applied, and the Auditor General has gone on from time to time, drawing the attention of the government to the defects in the law. He has refused to pass accounts which, in his judgment, contravened some provision of the law. He has debated the point with the department responsible for the expenditure, and after being overruled has gone to the Treasury Board and. debated the point with that board, and again and again has been overruled. We are bound to assume that the Auditor General is a conscientious official, anxious to do his duty faithfully. Again and again his decisions have been overruled, and he has continued to urge that money was paid out improperly. Bet me draw attention to a ease in point. We provided by a statute that when bridges were built which cost a certain amount, the government would contribute 15 per cent of their cost. The Auditor General deemed it his duty to ascertain whether the statement of cost was a cooked one. The government thought that in so doing he exceeded his duty, but he refused to accept that view and after some time he succeeded in having an in-
*

vestigation. What was the result ? It was found that the very account to which he objected was so made up as to show that the bridge cost a great deal more than it actually did, and had he passed the demand for payment, very many thousands of dollars would have been paid over to which they were not entitled. There is an evidence that the Auditor General is right in the stand he takes. The government contended that he had no business to inquire into the details ; and had the Auditor General submitted to that contention, the country would have been mulcted a considerable sum. Why should we not make the point clear by amending the Act so as to give him the right which he claims to have ? We are told by the Finance Minister that the Act contains ample powers. If that be the case, how is that year after year the Auditor General has disputes with almost every department over the payment of money, and almost invariably has been overruled and the money paid out ? Take the Davis contract, about which there is so much talk at present. What was the objection of the Auditor General in that matter ? In the first place he drew attention to what he regarded as a very unbusinesslike contract. He pointed to the fact that if he were to authorize the money to be paid, there would be thousands of dollars paid out in return for which the country got no service whatever.
Now, if that be a fair interpretation of the Act, if tliat might be done under the Act, would it yet be a proper thing to do ? When any one receives money, he receives it for consideration given, and when the country pays money it is supposed to receive something in return. But the fact was disclosed that there was no service rendered for that money. The contractor could not give the electric light because there was no connection with the power station-the power was there but it was not applied. Yet, an account was sent in of SI it000. Suppose that money had been paid out for nothing, would the country approve it ? Would the Finance Minister defend it ? And yet the hon. member for Scuth Brant (Mr. Heyd) stands up and reads the advice of Mr. Aylesworth that, according to the law, he does not see how the Auditor General can refuse, because the contract made with the Department of Railways and Canals said that the contractor should have so much money at a certain time it failed to provide that a service should be reudered before the government incurred obligations. So, according to Mr. Aylesworth, the Auditor General had no power under the Audit Act to check this payment. Well, do not you think he ought to ''nave that power ? Do not you think it would have been in the interest of the country to amend the Act so as to have given him that power ? I think so. And
the country has long since reached the conclusion that the Audit Act should be amended so as to give the Auditor General ample power to protect the treasury. Now, when the Auditor General checks payment of money and the payment is still presisted in, the matter is referred to the Treasury Board. Here is the clause of the statute :
If the Auditor General has refused to certify that a cheque of the Minister of Finance and Receiver General may issue, on the ground that the money is not justly due, or that it is, in excess of the authority granted by the council, or for any other reason than that there is no parliamentary authority, then upon a report of the case prepared by the Auditor General aud the Deputy of the Minister of Finance and Receiver General, the Treasury Board shall be the judge of the sufficiency of the Auditor General's objection and may sustain him or order the issue of the cheque in its discretion.
In this case they overruled him and ordered the money to be paid, we think, improperly. The Auditor General fell back upon two objections. He said, in the first place, the law provides, under section 11 of chapter 37 of the Consolidated Statutes, winch relates to the Department of Railways and Canals, how a contract shall be made. This section is as follows :
The minister shall invite tenders, by public advertisement, for the execution of all works, except in cases of pressing emergency.
Now, this was a case of lighting the Cornwall canal. It was clearly not a case of pressing emergency, for the lighting of the canal could go on under the system already in use when this contract was made. So the Auditor General contended that he had the rig'ht to refuse to allow the payment of that money unless other conditions were complied with. If the contract was not let by public tender, the deputy or the clerk in the department under whom the work is done or goods supplied, must certify that the work had been done or the goods received and that the values were reasonable. The Auditor General had no such certificate before him and he demanded the certificate. They refused to give it to him. So, the contract was not let by tender, and the work was not certified to as being good value. Therefore, the Auditor General conceived it to be his duty not to allow the public treasury to be raided and the money paid. Was he right or was he wrong ? Mr. Aylesworth said that, according to the Audit Act, the Auditor General could not check the payment of that money, the Treasury Board having overruled him. Why could he not check it ? Because the provisions of the Audit Act were not sufficiently strong. That is why we propose by this resolution that the Act should be amended and strengthened. We ask the government to take the matter up. We ask parliament to express its opinion. For it would be of no use for us to propose such a law ; we

could not carry it through. The Minister of Finance asks why, if there is any defect in the Audit Act the opposition do not introduce a Bill to amend it. I have suggested the reason. It would be only a waste of time. We have not the power to put through such a measure. And, besides, it is the government and not we who are charged with responsibility of directing public affairs. We are here to see to it tnat any measures which they propose shall be as nearly perfect as we can get the majority to make them. The opposition would willingly support a Bill to strengthen the Auditor General-they would have done it last year, and they are willing to do it at any time. We hold that the Auditor General ought to have as wide powers as are necessary to enable him to effectively protect the public treasury. Alexander Mackenzie said at one time that lie was like a soldier in the trenches, sleeping on his arms that he might be ready to protect the treasury against the incursions of those who desired to get that money of the public improperly. It was to provide relief for himself and those who might follow him that he asked parliament to pass an Act authorizing 'him to appoint an Auditor General. That Auditor General he appointed. He showed his desire to protect the public treasury so far as he thought the necessities of the situation demanded it. But experience has shown us ways in which that Act can be improved. My hon. friend says that the demand of the electors, after a quarter of a century's experience, is That this Act shall be improved. There is not a doubt that that is the feeling of the public. What is true of every other law is true of the Audit Act. Every year we place upon the statute-book, laws, which, in our judgment and to the best of our knowledge and of the experience we have, are sufficient. And yet further experience shows how those laws can be advantageously amended from time to time. Parliament, after careful inquiry exercises its judgment in voting money for public purposes, and then it is left to the Auditor General to see to it that the money is spent according to the intention of parliament. Now the Auditor General, I assume, never refused, from mere wilfulness, to give his certificate for the payment of money. Iam sure every one will credit him with honesty. And it is to be Supposed that he does not wilfully get into trouble or conflict with any department, or with the Treasury Board, or with the government. But, as an honest man he is bound to fight any or all of them if that is necessary in order to maintain the proper checks upon the expenditure of public money. And he has fought them for years, until he has become sick and tired of that job. And now he says: If you will not amend the Audit Act, if you will not Mr. SPROULE.	* .
place at my disposal proper provisions and assistance such as I require to safeguard tbe treasury, then, I want you to accept my resignation.
I, as an honest man, cannot hold the position unless I endeavour to do my duty
and if the government makes it impossible for me to do my duty, if they will not put within my reach provisions that will enable me to do my duty, I want at least to show the country that I desire to do right, and when I cannot do it I want to get out-and he has sent in his resignation. I say that the country to-day regards with great suspicion that resignation of the Auditor General. I venture to say that, irrespective of politics, forty-nine out of fifty of tbe electorate today will tell you honestly, if you ask them, that they are desirous of keeping the Auditor General them of strengthening his hands rather than weakening them. They desire to keep him there because he has shown his desire and his ability to protect the public treasury, he has shown his willingness and his honesty of purpose, he has shown that he	is prepared to
fight either party, his own party that put him in that position as well as the party that was opposed to him. He has shown honesty and a high sense of duty, and has endeavoured to do his duty. Will the country strengthen his hands, will the government strengthen his hands, or will they prevent him from doing his duty ? We know that in many instances the Treasury Board has overruled him, and instead of strengthening his hands have been weakening him, instead of giving him moral support they have been discrediting the man. aud his judgment, and his ways, killing the very means that were designed to protect the treasury of the country. Every obstacle it seems to me is being thrown in his way so as to make it impossible for him to do his duty as he conceives it should be done. Does the country 'want that ? In my judgment it does not.
The Auditor General has given fair and ample notice to the government; Unless you amend this Act, unless you support my authority, I want to get out. Are they going to let him get out ? If they do, the country will know the reason why. He has told us the reason why. We draw attention to it to-day so that the country may know, that parliament may understand. We do not desire to see the Auditor General get out, we desire him to remain there. But we desire also that the Act should be amended in any needful particular so as to make his powers, in the words of this resolution, ample to protect the public interest and safeguard the public treasury. He has appealed to parliament because the government has refused to support him. Is parliament going to be equal to the occasion ? Will the representatievs of the people do their duty ? We are endeavouring to do it

on this side of the House. Who are we opposed by ? By the very men who are charged with the responsibility of protecting the public treasury. We are working in the interests of the country, we are opposed by the very men whose duty above everything else in the world is to protect the country and to look after its interests. If this government and parliament refuse, what will be the inevitable result ? What conclusion will the people reach ? They can come to but one conclusion, and that is that the government do not desire to protect the public treasury as they should, that the government do not desire to strengthen the hands of the Auditor General, the employee of parliament, not the employee of the government, but the servant of the country. They do not wish to give him that moral support, that constitutional support which they above all others ought to give him to enable him to do his duty. Then I say if they fail in this matter we will appeal to the great parliament of the nation, we will lay this subject as fully as we can before the electors of the country, and I have no doubt that when they know the whole story, when they know that the Auditor General has been refused support, when they know that he has been antagonized by the present government, when they know that thousands and tens of thousands of dollars, yes I am within the mark in saying hundreds of thousands of dollars of government money, has been improperly paid out, money paid out for which the country never got anything in return-when the people know that, they will be very likely to blame the present government. I think it will take from them thousands of votes. I shall have no objection whatever if it results in putting them out. But I would rather see them do their duty and remain in, than to be kicked out for not doing their duty. I have that much respect for the Prime Minister who leads them. I believe there are some good men on that side of the House and some very bad ones. But they remind me of Sir Oliver Mowat and his friends. A number of them were said to be very good men and a number were said to be bad. He always had one man in his cabinet called the wicked partner who would father all the bad transactions, and Sir Oliver himself was the redeeming feature of the cabinet. But in this case the worst of it is that it is the bad element that seems to predominate all the time, the government leans over that way, the bad men control the elections, and the country does not get'the benefit of the good element in the cabinet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If we do as well as Sir Oliver Mowat, I do uot think Ontario will complain.

You mean by .holding on to power. I can only say [DOT] that the hon. gentleman and his friends are very apt followers, they seem to be falling into the same line very readily, especially in the work done by the wicked partner. The wicked partner seems to be on top here, and getting much more on top every day. That is why we want to set them right, or else give the country a chance to rectify the wrong. We intend to tell the country as plainly as we can, and if the government refuse* to do their duty as they seem inclined to to-day, they will have to suffer the consequences. Now for these reasons I am in favour of this resolution. I think we cannot pass it a day too soon. The Minister of Finance says :	Why did'nt you propose
this law three years ago Why did'nt you propose it two years ago ? Why did'nt you propose it last year ? Is it ever too late to meud ? It is true that in the interests of the country it might well have been proposed three years ago, or two years ago or last year ; but because of our laches in that respect are we to go on in the same line for ever ? When we know that a wrong is being done is it not high time that we amended our ways V Though it may appear late, even at the eleventh hour a repentant sinner may return. "It is because of our desire to do right that we propose this resolution to-day ; and I can only reach the conclusion that it is because of the government's desire to do wrong that they oppose it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Before the hon. gentleman takes his seat:	I understood
him to say that as a result of some imperfection in the Audit Act tens of thousands of dollars had been paid out without consideration. Will my hon. friend be good enough to give us some specific cases ?

I mentioned one with regard to the Sorel bridge. I mentioned one with regard to this contract, where the Auditor General shows that an application was made for over $52,000 and for the most of which there was no return given to the country whatever. It may have been a defect in the contract.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend ought to be aware of the fact that in neither case was there a dollar paid.

While there is not much disposition on the part of the government to treat this matter as one of sufficient importance to discuss it on this occasion, still there can be no doubt that in the opinion of the people of the country generally the Auditor General is the most useful official of the country. He is the gentleman who was spoken of as a very important official in the years when the Conservatives were in power, when this matter was discussed by leading and prominent members of the Liberal party, then in opposition. They said that he had an onerous duty to perform when he had the supervision of expenditure of probably $40,000,000. The importance of this proposition was emphasized by Liberal speakers at that time on account of the large amount of money in question. If that was a good argument previous to 1S96, it is manifestly much stronger to-day because now the expenditure of the country is almost double that expenditure of $40,000,000, and while it is true that the members of the administration to-day are disposed not to treat this discussion very seriously, but simply to pass it over, following apparently the line taken by the Minister of Finance in connection with it, that party did treat it seriously during the years when they were in opposition. I find that in 1895 the Hon. David Mills devoted a large part of a day in parliament to a resolution moved on a motion to go into supply, to a discussion of this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On the same lines ?
Not on the same lines.

speechtext: Will my hon. friend read the resolution ?

It does not seem to be included in the discussion in ' Hansard.' The discussion occurs at page 240S of the ' Hansard ' of 1895. On that occasion, I am bound to say, a different phase of the subject was treated. The point at issue then was an application of the Auditor General to the government and to parliament for assistance and relief. On that occasion, as nearly as I can gather from the speeches, the Auditor General was rather pleading for increased remuneration for his officials and increased power of control over the officials of his department. Therefore the discussion on that occasion was not by any means on all fours with this, but still it is evident from Mr. Mills's speech that he regarded this -official as being one of the [DOT]most important appointed by the govern-

ment of Canada. Ho presses particularly upon the attention of the House the fact referred to over and over again that the Auditor General is not at all an official of the government of Canada, but an official of the parliament and of the people of Canada. Mr. Mills in this discussion called attention to the fact that the duties of the Auditor General are twofold ; first, that he conducts an administrative audit in the interests of the people. That is to say, not only does he see that the various appropriations are so expended and accounted for and justified by voucher as to protect the administration, but he also sees that the government of the day uses these appropriations for the purposes for which they are voted by parliament so that there can be no question at all that on that occasion the Liberal party, as represented by Mr. Mills, gave a great deal of prominence to this feature of the case, that the Auditor General is to a certain extent exercising a supervision and control over the administration and for that reason it is urged in the course of that speech and elsewhere that that official should receive the most thorough and unlimited support from the parliament of Canada. In so far as this matter has been treated by the government on this occasion they have apparently made up their minds not to consider it very fully at this time. They have urged in the fitst place through the Finance Minister, as a reason for not considering it, that the time is not opportune, that the matter is brought to the notice of the House at a time when parliament has practically reached the conclusion of its business for this year. To my mind that cannot possibly be the reason why the government has decided not to come to the assistance of the Auditor General in this matter. If it were, it would involve our assenting to the proposition that they had no knowledge of this application of "the Auditor General until this matter was brought to their attention by the opposition. That, this House and the country know, is not the case. The Auditor General during every year, as is set forth at great length in the pages of his report, has been engaged in constant controversy with the government of the day, and so far as my reading has gone I must say, uniformly, in every case in which the Auditor General has felt it his duty to differ in opinion as to the appropriations made to the government, the government, relying on and using the authority of the Treasury Board, has overruled the Auditor General. I do not believe that any one in this House, particularly on this side of the House, is disposed to differ from the view laid down by the Finance Minister in so far as they will not consent for one moment to allow the Auditor General to assume the function of deciding the policy of this country. We are not disposed to part with one jot or title or particle of
that system which we have inherited, adopted and developed in this country under which every portion of the expenditure made by Canada must be made upon the authority of the government of the day. We do not for one moment contemplate nor see how it would be possible, or how any reasonable man for a moment could consider, that the functions of the government of Canada should be devolved upon any official, Auditor General or any one else, and therefore we, I think, are entirely at one with the government in insisting that nothing should be done to deprive the government of the day of any of its constitutional rights or powers. We look upon the responsibility of ministers to parliament and through them to the people as the basis of the system which we have inherited, which we have worked under in the past and which we must continue to work under. We do not -want any suggestions to come from the government side of the House that we are endeavouring in any way to interfere with constitutional practice. I do not think it would be possible for the minister to make it appear plain that the Auditor General, in the request he is making of the people of Canada-for he is appealing to the whole people of Canada-is asking them to give him the power of taking the government by the throat when he might see fit to do so, or to make him a final court of appeal to say when the government is doing right and when it is doing wrong. I do not think that the Auditor General has any such idea in his mind and if he had he would find no support for it on this side of the House.
I believe that the desire of the Auditor General would be to a large extent gratified by some such measure as that which has been outlined by the leader of the opposition today. The Auditor General thinks that under certain circumstances which come under his cognizance in a way to lead him to believe there has been an improvident bargain, he should be fortified to the extent that he could bring to his assistance a mode of investigation by which he could prepare himself to submit to the administration through the Minister of Finance, reasons which might induce the government to correct the defects in any contract. I do not think anything could be more appropriate for that "purpose than a reference to the Exchequer Court or to some other court in which information of a conclusive character could be derived from the examination of witnesses. There is at present in our system no means by which, if the administration of the day is disposed to be careless or prejudiced in favour of a contract, the Auditor General can make such an inquisition as would be necessary to bring before the government such information as might induce them to change their minds. We know that the people of this

country cannot have any first hand knowledge of such disputed questions, and that indeed it is hard for members of parliament to make discoveries in reference to such, because the report of the Auditor General is only in their hands twelve months or more after the transactions have been discovered. It seems to me that it would not at all be adverse to the principle of constitutional government and it would not be prejudicial to honest and economic administration in this country, if some provision were made by which the Auditor General might for a short time suspend the operation of a contract or the payment of an account until he could ascertain by some judicial process such information as would enable him to submit to the government a complete statement of his views, and of the grounds which might induce the administration to change their minds. While it may not have been intended, yet there is something disingenuous in the argument of the Minister of Finance, who does not consider the question at all, but who at once appeals to that strong sentiment in the House and in the country, which is opposed to any change which would deprive us of that system of ministerial responsibility upon which *we rest, and.must rest in this country. The Minister of Finance was simply begging the question. While I do not wish to pursue him into a detailed consideration of the Davis contract, out of the consideration of which probably this question has come to the surface, still, even in that case I would almost seem inclined to think that the Minister of Finance might find that there were some reasons which would make it advantageous to the administration to have the Auditor General, who stands between them and these persons to whom the money of the country is being paid, strengthened in his position. I should think that might be done not only in the public interest, but also for the comfort and convenience of the government itself. No harm could result by any extension of the powers of the Auditor General which stop short of confiding in him any authority superior to that of parliament, or of the ministry which parliament for the time being sustains in power. It would seem that the government would lia\ e done well if they liad copied the example of preceding administrations which have over and over again amended the Audit Act, and which have shown a disposition to strengthen the hands of the Auditor General in every constitutional manner. I would advise that this matter be treated not too lightly, because it is absolutely important for this administration and for succeeding administrations, that the people of Canada should know that the administration desires to have as sweeping an investigation as possible into the public accounts which any properly authorized ofll-cial like the Auditor General may insti-Mr. BELL.
tute. I was sorry to hear in the course of the discussion reference made to the suspicious character of the negotiations and contracts between Mr. Davis and succeeding governments in Canada. If such insinuations were made in the report of the Auditor General it was very unfortunate. It is most important that we should always extend to administrations in this country that generous treatment which we are disposed to extend even to criminals, and to believe them innocent until they are proven guilty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is awfully kind.

I do not think there could be a more unfortunate feature in our public life than that there should develop a disposition on the part of public men, or on the part of public organs to attempt to force on the minds of the people of this country, a predisposition to believe that there was a dishonest purpose on the part of any administration. We ought to assume, and we must assume, that our governments are pure. It is such a cheap, such an easy and such an abominable practice, to go on insinuating corrupt motives and corrupt acts on the part of an opponent, that to my mind every man who w'ishes a healthy sentiment in the public life of Canada, ought to discourage it to every extent in his power. We ought be willing to believe that the government of the day are doing what they can in the interests of the people. So far as I am concerned I have no sympathy with this casting of suspicions, and I regret that this matter should be discussed here at all. I do not believe there was any such corrupt bargain in the case I have referred to. I do not believe anything of the kind was intended, and if the Auditor General has introduced such an insinuation into the report he has gone entirely outside of his duties and functions, and has made a grave mistake. But, while that is the case, there can be no doubt that among the party organs on both sides, and probably among public men on both sides, there is a constant tendency to cover up their own faults by insinuating evil doing or corruption on the part of their opponents. Therefore it is to my mind in the interests of every succeeding administration of this country, to conduct our public affairs in such fashion that the people of the country shall learn to have confidence in the fact that the purpose of every succeeding government is to have the fullest and freest inquiry into all matters, so that the people of the country may always rest in confidence that the business of the country for the time being is honestly transacted. While it may not be an opportune time for the administration to engage in this work now, and while it may be enough to observe that we are approaching the end of a long session, still I

think it would be well for the administration to let it be understood that so far as they are concerned they have nothing to fear from any inquiry of any kind whatever which is conducted within proper constitutional limits by any official of the government or by anybody else. I am satisfied that this administration does not fear anything of the kind, and I believe it is in the interests not only of this government but of any government that may succeed, to make that point perfectly clear. If there is any weakness or any defect at all in the powers which the Auditor General has to discharge his duties, that defect should be repaired. So nearly as 1 can discover, the view which the Auditor General takes, and the view that all reasonable men take, is, that there may be a necessity to a certain extent, 1 do not know how far, to increase the powers of the Auditor General, to make inquiry under certain circumstances.
. If that be admitted there is a great justification for some change in the law which would enable the Auditor General to discharge his full functions under certain restrictions, which restrictions should be clearly stated and which should not be of such a nature as to admit of constant and unwarranted interference.
There should be some power granted to the officer whose duty it is to watch the expenditure. if he thinks a bargain has been made without sufficient knowledge ,of the circumstances, or that it is an improvident bargain, to suspend, for a certain time, action in the direction of payment, to enable him to institute such an inquiry as would satisfy him, and through him,'the people of the country that everything was being done that could be done to secure economical expenditure. That is, to my mind, aii that is asked for by my leader, both in the matter and in the manner in which he has introduced this question to parliament at this time. We know that the auditor was not always a feature of our politics, either in the mother country or in -Canada. There was a time, not very long ago, when there was no such office as an audit office either in Great Britain or in this country ; but no man to-day would, I think, suggest that wo should go back to those days and dispense with the audit office, and leave it entirely in the hands of an administration to satisfy the people as to the nature of the public expenditure by -simply appealing to the. country on the ground of their fitness, their character, their standing and their respect for themselves as an administration. It does not imply that a man or an administration is dishonest because you ask them to submit to certain checks and guards on expenditure. It is, to my mind, merely a proper course to follow in reference to the mul titudinous expenditures of this country, which no government can possibly supervise for itself, or in reference to the employment of the host of officials that we
have in Canada. No administration can thoroughly supervise for itself all the enormous expenditures of this country; the people cannot supervise them for themselves : and the members of parliament have no opportunity' of supervising them. We must retain the services of the Auditor General ; and when he shows a reasonable ground for the contention that he requires to have his powers increased, we should be ready to increase his powers. I feel that this is. not a matter which the opposition would be disposed to introduce as a contentious matter. It is too important ; it is above that ; it is a matter which the administration of the day should decide : but it is the duty of the opposition to bring it to the notice of the administration. There can be no question at all, I presume, that to-day, just as in the days when the Conservative party wore in power, the Auditor General looks upon the opposition as his natural allies. It is his business to watch the administration so far as their appropriations are concerned, and to watch the officials in so far as all the expenditures are concerned ; and it is only natural that he should regard the opposition of the day as his natural allies and assistants. In every ease where the Auditor General thought the government were not giving him such support as he felt himself entitled to, but on the contrary regarded him as rather overmeddling. as too carping and critical, as a man with whom, in course of time, they might grow somewhat out of patience, and to whom they might not turn a ready ear, nothing would be more natural than that he should either appeal to the country as a whole or take the natural course, during the time parliament is in session, of appealing to that body of people who constitute the opposition of the day. But, after all, this is a matter which it is the duty of the administration to deal with. If the administration can show, as they have not on this occasion attempted to show, that the Audit Act is amply effective and that there are no grounds whatever for any request on the part of the Auditor General or the opposition to improve it, then they are perfectly justified : but I do not think the government of the day -are altogether justified, when this matter is brought to their notice, in treating it as it has been treated by the administration on this occasion. It must be said that they have treated it with scant courtesy. The Finance Minister made a very-short speech. He did not profess to exert himself, but disposed of the whole subject as one which might be lightly brushed aside. He treated it as an attack by the apposition, and did not deal with the question in its broad aspects. He made only a brief reference to the particular contract out of which this whole question may be said to have taken its rise ; and, so far as tiiat particular contract was concerned, it seems to me the effect of the speech of the

Finance Minister was to justify the position of the Auditor General. The result would seem to go to show that by the intervention of the Auditor General the great purpose to which the people of the country are devoted -the economizing of the public funds-has been served. If that is true, it is a very powerful argument why some careful inquiries into this matter should be made.

I do not intend to occupy many minutes in the remarks that I propose to make on the subject now before the House. It is not, 1 think, necessary that I should do so. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition dealt fully with the outlines of the Bill which he suggested, and the reasons he gave for suggesting such a measure to the government, have not so far been answered. So far there has been no attempt whatever to reply to my hon. friend. It was a matter of surprise to me that the hon. the Minister of Finance should have avoided the substance of the question before the House, as he did, by referring to what he called the abstract motion of the leader of the opposition. The Minister of Finance knows perfectly well-no one knows better-why my hon. friend moved that abstract motion. He knew that the object of my hon. friend was to keep himself within the rules of the House. He knew that my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, made this abstract motion in order that he might lay before the government the draft or form of a Bill which could become law only if taken up by the government. There is nobody in this House who is not perfectly aware that if to-day a Bill of that character were introduced by anyone from this side, it would not have the slightest prospect of becoming law. There is no hon. member who does not know that the only chance such a Bill would have of getting upon the statute-books would be for the government of the day to take it up and put it through the House. It was for that reason that the leader of the opposition took the particular method he did, and laid before the House and the country a proposition that I think the government ought to have accepted. In the course of his remarks, the leader of the opposition said that he was not wedded to the particular wording of the Bill. He did not care exactly in what words the subject matter was expressed. All he proposed was to lay before the House what he thought was required as an improvement to the Audit Act and to leave to the government to adopt what phraseology they pleased, so long as they gave effect to what he considered was required. Therefore the Bill is before the Mr. BELL.
House, to all intents and purposes, as fully as if it had been introduced in the ordinary course. Everybody knows how impossible it would be for this side to have such a measure adopted. The only possible way of its becoming law would be for hon, gentlemen opposite to take up the measure we suggest. That suggestion has been made, and we are waiting yet for some reply to the remarks which the hon. the leader of the opposition gave in support of the measure he outlined.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance pleaded the right of parliament to do wrong if it chose and deprecated any limitation of its functions. Those are in effect the words he used. Well, we could not restrain or limit the powers of parliament even if we desired to do so. Nobody contends that it is possible for us to restrain or affect or limit parliamentary power. But I would like to ask this of the Finance Minister. Would he be good enough to state what sentence there is, from the beginning to the end of the proposition made by the leader of the opposition, which can be in any way construed as an attempt to interfere with the powers of parliament. Every passage of the Bill we propose, shows that' there is not the slightest intention on the part of anybody to interfere with the fullest control by parliament. On the contrary what the leader of the opposition wants, is that parliament shall have the means of itself dealing with the subject. He does not want to give to any judge or auditor the power which parliament itself alone should exercise. In what possible manner can the proposed Bill interfere with the powers of parliament ? What is the proposition ? It is that in the event of the auditor appointed by this House and acting for this House, being of the opinion that the occasion called for such action on his part, he could petition the judge of the Exchequer Court to investigate certain matters that have come before him as auditor. The proposition is not that the judge shall deal with the question, not that he shall decide as between the government and the party claiming money, but that he shall investigate and report to parliament for the action of parliament. Surely in the face of such a proposition, the contention of the Finance Minister that we are endeavouring to get rid of the paramount authority of parliament is simply absurd. On the contrary we are endeavouring to increase the effective power of parliament. We are endeavouring to give parliament the means of dealing with matters which are now dealt with in the cabinet and secretly.
The Minister of Finance says that he cannot vote for the motion of the leader of the opposition, because it implies that the powers under the Audit Act are not now sufficient. In effect

he contends that the Audit Act, passed many years ago under conditions very different indeed from those of to-day, cannot be improved to meet the circumstances in which iwe now live. Well, Sir, I 'have heard of Conservatism and Old Toryism, but for for such a proposition as this to come from a Liberal and a member of a Liberal government is certainly an extraordinary thing. Would it not be an improvement to provide that, when the Treasury Board overrule the Auditor General, the officer of parliament, they shall give reasons for that overruling ? That is one of the propositions of the hon. leader of the opposition. If that were adopted, the report of the Auditor General-and he is bound to report to parliament the overrulings of the Treasury Board *-would give us not only the fact of the overruling but the reasons for it. Would anybody say that that would not be an improvement ? We read, session after session, Treasury Board decisions simply telling us that the Treasury Board do not approve the action of the Auditor General and overruling that action. That is all that is told us. These gentlemen may be right or they may be wrong, but, in their magnificence they are altogether above informing us why they take the particular view they do. Now the Auditor General, I say again is*an officer of parliament, not an officer of the government; he is put there to overlook the expenditure of the government. He has before him in some particular case, the claim of a contractor or other person for a sum of money and the voucher and certificate of one of the ministers,' the head of one of fhe departments of the government. Looking into the case he comes to the con-;clusion that there is something wrong- not necessarily something dishonest, we need not go into questions of dishonesty here, but something imprudent, informal, or, perhaps irregular-in the contracting of the debt. He refuses, acting for the public, to certify for the payment of the money. Well, what is done ? The Auditor General is overruled. By whom ? Why, by a committee or board of the gentlemen he is set to watch, by the Treasury Board, consisting of members of the cabinet. The public who trust the Auditor General are so particular about his independence that they will not allow the government to discharge him but provide that he is to be discharged only by parliament itself. But his decision is overruled by the colleagues of the head of the department *who demands the money. So far, good, perhaps. I quite admit that in public affairs it would be impossible to leave it to any Auditor General or any other officer, no matter who he may be to have the last word in relation to expenditure of money. Nobody disputes the honesty of the Auditor General, but people may sometimes doubt his judgment. He is only human. Therefore, it would be wrong to
make him a Czar and give him the right to say finally that moneys shall or shall not be paid. But, when he is overruled by an interested body, by the government of the day, who perhaps not dishonestly, but for reasons of their own, want the money paid, is that to be the end of it ? It would not be right, it would not be in the public interest that the Auditor General should be absolute; but is it in the public interest that the ministers should be absolute ? Is It to be for all time to come, with the growing importance of the transactions in this country, that a difference of opinion between the Auditor General and the minister is to be absolutly decided by the minister, through the minister's colleagues 1 Surely, if that is to be the case, there is little essentially good in the auditorship. It is quite true the Auditor reports the overruling to parliament. But that overruling is reported to parliament after the transaction is closed, because the Treasury Board have the power to order the money to be paid and without giving reasons. We ask, therefore, on this branch of the Bill, that, when the Auditor General is overruled the reasons for the overruling shall be stated, in order that when the report is made to parliament, we shall know not only why the Auditor General has objected but why his objection has been set aside.
Then, we contend that some special remedy should be provided for extreme cases, and I will refer to that later on. Nobody pretends-the leader of the opposition would be the last to pretend-that this special remedy was to be used for every occasion. It is not probable, it is not even possible, that it will come in to frequent use. Because, the Auditor General is an officer of parliament and If he is found to bring up every petty question before parliament, parliament will very soon deal with an officious petty officer of that kind who cannot appreciate the significance or importance of particular transactions under his consideration.
Now. Sir, the requirement of the reasons for overruling is not the only amendment that has been suggested. Section 48 of the Audit Act was evidently framed for the purpose of enabling the Auditor General, from time to time, to make suggestions to parliament. It was, no doubt, foreseen that, however careful parliament *might be in the framing of the Audit Act, many things would occur in the experience of an auditor which might well be reported to parliament for its consideration. Therefore, section 48 of the Act was inserted as ja sort of safety valve, if I may so call it, and a very useful one it is in my opinion. Now, section 48 as it stands in the Act today, enables the Auditor General to make special reports to parliament. As the Act stands it reads thus :

Now, upon that subject let me say a few words. We have again and again discussed in this House the proper application of expenditure for capital and for revenue. We find, in passing the estimates every year, that large sums are granted on capital account. It is impossible, when the estimates are before the House, however anxious gentlemen here may be to do their duty, to kuow whether the whole of that money is properly chargeable to capital or not. The government obtains a grant for, say, half a million of money applicable to a certain line of expenditure, and to be charged to capital. For example, in the railway grants a sum of three or four hundred thousand dollars may be applicable to expenditure upon bridges, and half a million in some years has been granted on capital account ifor steel rails. Now, no one in this House, when the estimates are passed, can undertake to say absolutely how much of that should be capital and how much revenue. But when the accounts come before the Auditor General after the expenditure has taken place, the Auditor General can tell that and can, by obtaining expert advice, know very closely indeed how much of that money should have been really charged to capital and how much to revenue. But as the statute has already been passed upon the estimates, making it all applicable to capital, he. as auditor, has nothing to do with it; all he can say is that ¥500,000 has been expended upon rails and $350,000 upon bridges, and upon the Act which was passed by parliament he is directed to charge all Mr. BARKER.
to capital. Now, I say that the Auditor General, while carrying out strictly, according to his duty, what parliament has directed him to do. that is to charge that money up to capital, should be enabled and required to report to this House specially that it has come to his knowledge in the investigation of the accounts that a portion, perhaps all, of that which was so charged to capital ought really to have been charged to revenue account. Can anybody dispute that this is an important feature of auditing ? The Auditor General cannot help us as the Audit Act stands. The estimates have been passed, they have become an Act of parliament. He is directed to charge a certain expenditure to capital, and he must obey, though he finds in the course of the year that the government is renewing bridges with that capital appropriation. The estimates for the public service are prepared each year in each department by the officials of that department, and after these estimates have received the approval of the head of the department, they are brought down to parliament. When they come to parliament they are fully discussed. Every item is open to public discussion and must be justified. And we who have sat in this House the last few years know that the severe critics of the opposition will insist on almost every dollar of every item being justified before the item is allowed to pass.
