And I take it that if there is any wrong-doing in connection with anything for which the government is responsible, the remedy is not to be found in making idle, vain charges. For, after all, we must bear in mind that slander and libel will travel miles while truth is getting its boots on. We must not overlook the fact that unfortunately there are those in this country who are too prone to believe everything wrong as concerning public men. There are those in this country-and I speak of both sides of politics-who are too prone to believe that every man who comes to this House comes for his own personal profit and his own personal advantage. And I say that that is not fair to the public men o? Canada; it is not fair to the men who occupy positions in this,House to proceed, by insinuation. to suggest wrong-doing. The proper course is to make a statement and, having made it. to abide by the consequences after a full and fair investigation.
Now, I have, perhaps, travelled further than I had intended to do and further than I ought to have done. But, briefly, the view l take is this, that so far as the Audit Act is concerned, that Act now contains all that is necessary to enable the Auditor General to carry on the duties which it was originally intended he should perform. If to enable him to more faithfully perform those duties amendments are required, the government would be, not only willing, but anxious to do anything necessary to facilitate his task. But I say it is not by substituting the courts for parliament that we can accomplish that object. And, so far as the Auditor General is concerned, I repeat what I said a moment ago : I have no quarrel with him personally, but he is too much of a man, I assume, and too vain of his own opinion, not to see that people who differ from him should not be afraid to declare their differences. And when I come to discuss the matter further, I shall have occasion to point out inaccuracies in connection with the statement in connection with the Davis contract far more serious and more important than the one pointed out by the leader of the opposition this morning.

I am not about to discuss the legal phase of this question.
I have listened attentively to the speeches made this afternoon and this evening. I was especially struck with the speech of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick). I do not wish to flatter him, but he has thrown more light on yiis subject, for me at least, than anybody else who has spoken.
I was pleased to hear him say that the government is willing and anxious to amend the Audit Act. If that is done I think that is all the present auditor will require. Now I think if an inquiry is made, I have no doubt it will satisfy the Auditor. I think he is not an uureasonable*man, if he had been he would not have occupied that position for 26 years. He was appointed by Mr. Mackenzie when premier of this country, he was well known to the premier, he sat in this House, he was*a useful member of this House, he was the best mathematician in this country, and would not have received the appointment if he had been an inferior man. His services were needed at that time. The country was being robbed right and left, according to what Mr. Mackenzie himself said. He said he had all he could do, he had to stand guard over the public chest to keep the thieves away. That is why he appointed a man of the stamp of Mr. McDougall. Then when the Conservatives came into power four or five years after, and during the 18 years they remained in power, they retained the services of Mr. McDou-gali, they held up both his hands, and I never heard they had any accusation1 against him. I never heard that the opposition of that day had very much against | him either. So he must have been a pretty good man in that oflice. The Minis-

ter of Justice tells us this evening what an able officer he is, how he has gone down to the Cornwall canal, taking engineers with him, and made a thorough investigation as to the lighting of that canal by these lamps, and ascertaining whether the government were paying too much for them. 30 cents a night seems to me to be altogether too much. However, that is not my business except as a member of this House whose duty it is to see that we do not pay more than a thing is worth. The government should inquire into this matter, they should have inquired long ago whether the previous government had made a foolish bargain. or not. It seems to me rather late in the day to make these inquiries. However, the Auditor tells us that they are paying too much, and if so, then I think the government ought to assist him with a view of paying only what is right. I think it is our duty to maintain the present Auditor in his office. It will cost us less. If you superannuate him-he is only 65 years of age and he is good for ten years more-if you superannuate him you will have to pay him almost as much money as the next Auditor will get, that is, you will have to pay two auditors and you only require one. He is quite able and competent to discharge those duties, so I think the government had better amend the law ; he is asking nothing unreasonable and I think the government should do it. Now speaking of auditors, do not the farmers, does not everybody in this country know what auditing means and what it costs ? Why, Sir, there is not a village, town, township or county, or a loan society, or any other business corporation but requires an auditor to look into its financial affairs. Some business corporations have lost hundreds of thousands of dollars by inefficient auditors. Now when you have a may whom the whole people of this country respect, in whom you have full confidence, try and keep him as long as you can. Why, Sir, it is to my own knowledge that one loan company in a town near where I liwe have lost thousands and thousands of doliars through an inefficient auditor. I am pretty sure that the government will take this matter up. I am speaking on their behalf, I sympathize with them ; I do not want them to go to the country with this affair hanging over their heads, having to meet the charge that they have thrown out the most efficient auditor this country ever had for the purpose of putting some man in his place that is anxious for the job. That is what they will surely be charged with if they let him go.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we proceed in committee with the estimates which have already been under consideration, I have a suggestion to make as respects which I have had a conversation with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), and in which I. think I shall have his concurrence. Our session has now advanced into the new fiscal year and we have no supplies voted. From day to day claims will come in for the services of the current year, some of which may not be very urgent, but many of which are* of a character that cannot conveniently be postponed. That would notably be the case in regard to the civil service and the payment of labour generally. In the ease of larger claims, perhaps, no serious harm would come from a little delay, but it is very inconvenient to have claims of that character delayed even for a very short time. I have therefore to propose that the committee shall grant us what is called a ' vote on account ' to the extent of one-fifth of the items that have not already been dealt with by the committee. We have dealt with a number of items which now stand on the order paper for concurrence. At the earliest possible moment I will ask the House to concur in these items and I would besides now ask the committee to favour us with this general vote of one-fifth of the items which have'not yet been considered. I quite realize that in asking the committee to make this appropriation, it is necessary to have an understanding as to the effect of the committee granting this vote on account. Many of these items may possibly be the subject of consideration and debate. It is quite possible that some
gentlemen may wish to object to some of them and therefore it should be perfectly understood that in voting for this one-fifth, as a matter of urgency, no hon. gentleman should be held as committing himself to the expenditure, but that every member should be absolutely free to discuss the matter as fully as if this vote had not been passed. It is a matter of urgency, it has been done on a number of occasions in past years and I hope I shall have the concurrence of hon. gentlemen opposite in meeting these urgent claims in the way I have suggested. I therefore beg to move that
A sum not exceeding the amount set forth below, be granted to His Majesty for the following services for the year ending the 30th June, 1905

Then we set forth all the items not yet dealt with and take one-fifth in each case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The same question arose last session and I then satisfied myself that it had been the practice, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has just stated, to concur in such a vote on account It is thoroughly understood, as I thought it was thoroughly understood last year, that in assenting to this vote for reasons which are in the public interest, we are not in any way depriving ourselves of the right to object to any item or to discuss to the fullest possible extent any of the items, a vote on account of which is thus given. In order that there may be no possible misunderstanding on that subject,
L now express my concurrence in what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has said. We are voting these items not because we have considered them, not because we are prepared to approve of them all, but because they are submitted by the government and no doubt will eventually be passed, and for public reasons it is necessary that many of them at least should be passed in this manner, in order that the public service might not suffer. In that view and only in that view, I assent to the proposal which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has just made.

I wish o^ice more to enter my protest against the causes which have made it necessary to have this vote pn account taken. That necessity is brought about by the late date at which parliament is called together, and I enter my protest most strongly against the present practice as I did last session ; at that time, I procured from Hansard ' that the premier when in opposition held views expressed by myself on this matter. Coming as I do from one of the outlaying portions of this country, coming here at a great sacrifice, at a season when every man who has any business to attend to should be at home looking after it, coming here in the spring and staying here away into the summer and fall as we have been doing for the past few years, and 1 as we seem likely to continue to do. I once

Mr. SI'ROT'LE. We have been repeatedly challenged across the floor of the House for allowing all votes to pass without objecting to them. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I euti ely concur in the view of my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) that in passing these items, no member is to feel that he is committing himself or in any way restricting his freedom of discussion.

Would not the Minister of Finance make some reply to my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) in regard to the holding of the sessions ? I am firmly of opinion that a great improvement can be made in the conduct of the business of this House and also in the time of year at which the House is called together. I heard the hon. member from the

western province (Mr. Boydi make the same protest last year ; I have heard him make it again to-night, and I think that every man in this House is of opinion that some improvement can be made and the protest having been entered, I think we are entitled to some statement from the government that they will seriously consider this protest and endeavour to arrange the public business so that it can go through with greater facility. These prolonged sessions are getting to be a serious thing for the members of this House. I feel it, and a great many hon. members in this House feel it, and we are looking for some kind of relief. It would be well worth the consideration of perhaps a joint committee to try in some way to improve the present condition of affairs.

The relief which my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) seeks may probably be obtained before the next session of the House, because if the government ventures on a general election, it will be no longer in their power to fix the time for the calling of parliament.
You have another guess.

Hughes). As a specimen of cold blooded nerve, the appearance of these two gentlemen on the scene at this particular stage of the game, beats the record. It is not by any means the sole reason why we are here in mid-summer when we should be at home attending to our business. If the length of this session has been a burden to the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) and to the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Now, I would like to say a few words with respect to the prolonging of this session. I want to tell my hon. friend from Alberta that if it were left to that hon. gentleman to criticise or find fault with any action of the government, we would find him minus his independent spirit, except of course when it suited himself. On this occasion it evidently suits him to rise in his place and defend the government and condemn hon. gentlemen on this side of the House for doing what they consider their duty. When the election takes place it is certain that hon. gentlemen opposite ' will find fault with the opposition for not criticising the public accounts. They will assert tuat we did not record our votes against the expenditure of this government. We are from day to day doing what we believe to be our duty in drawing the attention of the government to certain improper expenditures. So long as we are here we propose to continue in that course, and we do not propose to be lectured by the hon. member for Alberta. If that is the extent of his independence, we would ask him to kindly remain silent for the balance of the session, while we proceed with what we believe to be our duty. It is true, that the criticism on the estimates is confined to a comparatively few members on this side of the House; but I think we can claim the credit Mr. OLIVER.
of having at least as many men capable of criticising the estimates as hon. gentlemen opposite had when they were in opposition. We can say this also with a great deal of pleasure, that our criticism has been carried on in a gentlemanly manner. We have not used the language which the hon. gentleman's friends used previous to 1896. We have used language that has been strictly parliamentary and that we are not ashamed of, and in criticising these estimates we propose to continue in the same tone of language. Hon. gentlemen blame the opposition for extending the session. I want to know from the government if they are assisting in shortening the session by retaining to this late date certain public measures which we find on the order paper-no 'less than seven measures? Are we to blame because these measures have not been brought down ? Every hon. gentleman knows that in connection with constitutional government in this country or in any other, one of the weapons the opposition have in their hands is the estimates. Why do they reserve the right to criticise these estimates? First, to object to any unreasonable expenditure; and, secondly, as a means of hastening the government to bring down their measures in order that the opposition and the country may know what they propose to lay before parliament. All this is our right and duty, which we intend to exercise and we do not intend for one moment to tolerate any interference with our rights so long as we are exercising them in what we believe to be the best interests of the people of this country.
I just rise to say that I am very glad the hori. gentleman does not approve of the remarks I have made. They were not made with the view of securing his approval.

Perhaps the minister would explain the position of the government in so far as this contract is concerned ? Why did they extend the term of the original contract given in 1896 ? Why were changes made ? The minister should be able to give us a full statement of this whole matter, because it looks a very questionable one.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I was sympathizing with the complaints made regarding the length of the session and therefore was not going to inflict on the committee any very lengthy details. But it seems to me that the whole matter has been explained, and the explanation has been repeated iso often that it would be like imposing on good nature to inflict it again upon the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: I know how long suffering my hon. friend is, but it seems to me it is only a diseased mind which could suspect anything wrong in connection with this transaction. I think I have explained why the $26,500 are required, and it is for my hon. friends opposite to _sliow why it should not be voted. Having shown that the money is absolutely necessary, there should be no question about passing the vote.

I have asked the minister a reasonable question and he states, that on account of the length of the session he does not feel like inflicting any further explanation on the House. In fact, he treats the whole matter as a joke. But let me tell him that in 1896 the government then in
power entered into a contract for the lighting of the Cornwall canal for twenty-one years. In addition it was specified in that contract that the government were to pay 30 cents per light for the number of lights that would be required, a certain amount per horse-power for any horsepower required, and they were to have the right to expropriate the whole property at any time on paying five per cent over the original cost. Under that contract the government were not compelled to take the power or any of the lights unless they saw fit to do so. They might establish another waterpower if they chose and run their own lights or in any other way take power to open or manage their gates themselves. They simply specified that if they wished to work under this contract, they might do so. However, nothing was acted upon under that contract until the year 1900, just before the elections. At that time an Order in Council was passed by the government stipulating that there must be 250 arc lights placed on that Cornwall canal at a cost of 30 cents per light per night for the whole 365 days of the year. Thus the total cost for simply lighting the Cornwall canal was $27,375 per year. In addition an Order in Council was passed stipulating that the government should take 400 horse-power per annum for operating the locks, gates and bridges, at a cost of $63 per horse-power or $25,200 per annum. The government were thus to pay $52,500 per annum for lighting and operating the lock gates on the Cornwall canal. That is the contract which was made by the government now in office. These 400 horsepower which the government were to use for operating the locks, gates and bridges would only be used nine months in the year. They could not be used during the winter months, as neither gates nor the bridges are then opened. So that the stipulations of $63 per annum per horse-power really meant $63 per nine months. When this government were thus changing the contract and making a contract different from that passed in 1896, why did they not contract only to pay for this horse-power during the time it was used ? Because in making the rate $63 per annum, when they were only to use the power during nine months, they were really paying at the rate of $80 per annum. But that was not the most serious point. In addition they also passed an Order in Council extending the duration of the contract from 21 years to 84 years, or until 1979. Was there any reason why this contract should be extended ? Surely if the contractor had a contract for 21 years, that was quite long enough. That time, I should think as a member of this House, was sufficient; it was as much as any contractor could reasonably expect from the government or from a private concern.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I made this statement a month ago, and I think now the time has come to speak with absolute frankness and candour in connection with this matter. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That is another question. The question now under consider-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
ation is whether or not there has been any departure from the terms of the original agreement with respect to the extension in any respect whatever. I say there has not been.
Oh, oh.

speechtext: Evidently imperfect knowledge is the trouble in connection with this whole matter.

-to the satisfaction of the chief engineer of railways and canals, as may by the said engineer be from time to time required in writing for the working of the locks and other purposes.

All the second contract of 1900 did was to put into effect the original contract, and to do that which the original contract contemplated ; that is to say, to fix the number of lights and the number of horse-power as recommended by the chief engineer. That was what was done and that is all that was done. When we come to deal with the other contract as to the change we can easily deal with that, but one thing at a time. My hon. friend the leader "of the opposition asked me as to whether or not the original contract provided for the renewal of the right to supply horse-power for four consecutive periods amounting to 84 years, or whether or not the original contract had merely in contemplation the right to a lease of the power and of the land. The original contract had in contemplation lease of the power and of the land for 84 years ; that is to say, the government parted with possession of the land and parted with possession of the power, and the original contract contemplated that Davis should supply electric light and should als~ supply 2121
electric power. On page 11 you will find the contract that we have made with Mr. Davis in 1900, and you will find in this contract that after having made provision for the number of lights and the number of horse-power, it is said :
Nothing herein shall be taken to vary, other than as above specified or provided, any of the provisions of the said indenture.

speechtext: Well, I do not think my hon. friend is quite fair to me. He and I get along very well together, and it is not treating me very handsomely to tell me, after I have been trying to explain this one point for an hour, that I have not given an explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No doubt.

speechtext:

. Mr. J. D. REID. You pay $52,000 a year for lighting the Cornwall canal and for horse-power to move the gates.

speechtext: To move the gates and the bridges ; and there are the workshops and quite a number of things.
